## Introduction

Living systems persist through continual change. Molecules are replaced, structures are remodelled, environments fluctuate, damage occurs, and developmental transformations alter organisms across time. Yet living organisation can remain continuous through these changes.

This continuity cannot be understood simply as the retention of a fixed state.

APS describes the relevant phenomenon as **organised persistence**: the continuity of living organisation through change. Biological Agency, by contrast, identifies **viability-oriented organisational activity** (Spencer 2026).

The relationship between the two requires care.

Agency does not stand outside living organisation and cause persistence. Nor does organised persistence arise as the next stage in a sequence beginning with Agency. Agency and organised persistence provide analytically distinguishable perspectives on the same living organisation.

Agency asks what living systems do. Organised persistence identifies the continuity of living organisation that must be explained across change.

Activities analysed under Agency can nevertheless make a material difference to that continuity. Regulation can counter perturbation. Repair can restore damaged organisation. Compensatory activity can maintain viable conditions. Reorganisation can establish new ways of continuing when previous arrangements no longer suffice.

The central question of this article is therefore:

> **What is the explanatory relationship between present-tense viability-oriented Agency and the organised persistence of living organisation through change?**

APS answers that question without reducing persistence to Agency or turning Agency into an independent causal force.

## Where This Article Fits

This article is an Extension article within the APS Agency corpus.

It does not establish what biological Agency is or determine where Agency should be attributed. Those functions belong to **Biological Agency as the Activity of Self-Maintenance**, the canonical Agency Anchor.

Nor does it ask why Agency is the defining activity of Life or why biological Agency does not require intention or cognition. Those questions are addressed respectively in **Agency as the Defining Activity of Life** and **Agency Without Intentions**.

The present article addresses a different relationship: **how present-tense viability-oriented Agency relates to the organised continuity of living organisation through change.**

Agency and organised persistence are not successive stages in a causal sequence. Agency identifies viability-oriented organisational activity; organised persistence identifies continuity of living organisation despite material, structural, physiological, developmental, and environmental change.

This article therefore examines how activities analysed under Agency can contribute materially to maintaining and re-establishing conditions of continuity without treating Agency as an independent cause or sufficient explanation of persistence.

The relationship between present-tense Agency and historical evolutionary transformation is a further question and is not developed here.

## 1. Agency and Organised Persistence

Persistence can mean little more than continued existence through time. A rock may persist because enough of its structure remains unchanged. Living systems present a different explanatory problem.

Their material constituents turn over. Their internal conditions fluctuate. Their structures can be repaired and remodelled. Their relations with their environments change. Development can transform their organisation substantially while continuity is nevertheless maintained.

Living persistence is therefore not adequately characterised by duration alone.

**Organised persistence concerns the continuity of living organisation through change.**

Agency addresses that same organisation under a different explanatory projection:

> **Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity.**

These definitions should not be converted into a sequence.

Agency does not first generate viability, which subsequently produces persistence. Nor does a pre-existing organisation generate Agency as an additional capacity through which persistence is then achieved.

Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation. Agency identifies what that living organisation does. Organised persistence identifies its continuity through change.

The distinction is analytic, but it is not merely verbal.

Some activities of living systems make a material difference to whether viable organisation continues. Regulation, repair, compensation, and reorganisation can alter the consequences of perturbation. Their failure can likewise contribute to loss of viability and eventual breakdown.

Agency therefore matters to organised persistence because viability-oriented activity can participate materially in maintaining and re-establishing conditions under which living organisation continues.

This does not make Agency the whole explanation of persistence.

## 2. Continuity Is Not the Preservation of a Fixed State

A common image of persistence is stability: something persists because it remains sufficiently unchanged.

That model is inadequate for much of biology.

Living systems frequently maintain continuity by changing.

Development provides an obvious example. An organism does not remain in the same structural or physiological state from embryo to adult. Growth and differentiation alter its organisation profoundly. Yet these transformations need not interrupt the continuity of the living organism.

Repair provides another example. Following injury, persistence cannot always be maintained simply by protecting the remaining state. Damaged relations may have to be restored, replaced, compensated for, or reorganised.

Physiological regulation likewise need not return a system to an invariant condition. Changing circumstances can require altered patterns of activity if viable organisation is to continue.

Organised persistence therefore permitsâ€”and often requiresâ€”transformation.

The important explanatory question is not:

> How does the system prevent change?

It is:

> **How is continuity of living organisation maintained or re-established through change?**

This is where Agency becomes particularly relevant.

Viability-oriented activity can alter what happens under changing conditions. Living systems can regulate, repair, compensate, and reorganise. Such activities can contribute to continuity precisely because they need not preserve every previous state or relation.

Persistence is therefore compatible with substantial change in the organisation through which persistence is maintained.

## 3. Maintenance and Re-establishment

The distinction between **maintenance** and **re-establishment** is important.

Some biological activity maintains conditions already compatible with viability. Regulatory processes can limit departures from viable ranges, maintain necessary relations among processes, or compensate for ordinary fluctuations.

Other circumstances involve disruption that cannot be handled merely by maintaining the existing arrangement.

Damage may require repair. Loss of a structure may require regeneration or compensation. Environmental change may render an established activity ineffective. Development may require the replacement of one viable organisation by another while continuity of the organism is preserved.

In such cases, continuity depends upon re-establishing conditions of viability rather than simply retaining them.

This is why the canonical APS account of Agency includes both maintenance and re-establishment.

The distinction also prevents organised persistence from becoming synonymous with homeostasis. Living continuity is not exhausted by returning variables to fixed values. The organisation through which viable conditions are maintained can itself change.

Agency provides one analytic perspective on the activity involved in these transitions.

But again, Agency should not be treated as a separate entity performing maintenance upon an otherwise passive organisation. Regulation, repair, and reorganisation are materially realised activities of the living organisation itself.

Agency names their viability-oriented organisational character where that attribution is warranted.

## 4. Reconstruction Through Change

Some forms of continuity are best understood as reconstruction.

This does not mean that an organism is repeatedly destroyed and recreated. It means that continuity can depend upon replacing, repairing, or reorganising relations while preserving the living organisation relevant to the explanandum.

The distinction is particularly clear when a previous configuration can no longer support viable continuation.

A damaged tissue may be repaired through processes that produce structures different in detail from those present before injury. Developmental transitions can reorganise physiology and behaviour. Compensatory changes can redistribute functional contributions after disruption. Organisms can alter patterns of interaction with changing environmental conditions.

What persists in such cases is not necessarily every component, structure, activity, or relation.

The explanatory task is to determine **which organisation remains continuous, which changes are compatible with that continuity, and which materially realised activities contribute to maintaining or re-establishing it**.

Agency therefore does not mean preservation against change.

Viability-oriented activity can contribute to persistence by enabling change.

This gives organised persistence its dynamic character: continuity is compatible withâ€”and sometimes dependent uponâ€”the transformation of the organisation through which continuity is realised.

## 5. Constraints and the Organisation of Activity

Living activity is not an undifferentiated flow.

Material processes are channelled, enabled, and limited through constraints. In living systems, relevant constraints can participate in an organisation through which conditions of viability are maintained and re-established (Moreno and Mossio 2015).

This does not place constraint organisation before Agency in a causal sequence.

Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation. Agency is an analytic projection of that living organisation concerned with its viability-oriented activity.

The relevant question for this article is therefore narrower: **how do materially implemented constraints organise activities that make a difference to continuity?**

A regulatory relation can constrain processes so that perturbations are countered. Structural relations can enable repair. Changing constraints can alter the range of activities available under new conditions. Reorganisation can modify how processes are coupled when previous arrangements cease to support viability.

These are not examples of constraints acting separately from Agency.

They identify material relations through which viability-oriented activity is realised.

Likewise, Agency should not be described as an additional force that acts upon constraints. Where living systems modulate constraints, that modulation is itself materially implemented within the organisation whose continuity is being explained.

Constraint organisation therefore helps specify **how** particular instances of viability-oriented activity are realised without becoming a separate component paired with Agency.

## 6. Viability and Normativity

The relationship between Agency and organised persistence is viability-relative.

Not every possible condition is equivalent for living organisation. Some conditions support continued functioning; others impair it. Some perturbations can be accommodated; others exceed the organisation's capacity to maintain or re-establish viable conditions.

APS describes this asymmetry as **viability-relative normativity**.

No intention or conscious judgment is implied.

Accounts of biological autonomy and adaptivity have similarly connected agency with the capacity of living organisation to regulate activity relative to conditions bearing upon its continued viability (Di Paolo 2005).

The relevance of normativity here is limited but important. It explains why activities associated with maintenance, repair, and reorganisation are not merely changes among biologically equivalent states.

Their consequences differ relative to the continuation of the living organisation.

A repair process may restore conditions compatible with continued functioning. A compensatory response may prevent a perturbation from becoming destructive. A regulatory failure may move organisation beyond conditions from which viable functioning can be re-established.

These differences matter biologically because of their relation to viability.

Agency therefore concerns activity oriented within a field in which possible conditions are not equivalent for continued organisation.

Organised persistence concerns the continuity whose maintenance or loss gives those differences their explanatory importance.

## 7. Agency, Evaluation, and Significance

Viability-relative differences can acquire significance for a living system.

APS distinguishes this from Agency itself.

**Biological Evaluation is the process through which agency generates significance.**

The distinction prevents the Agencyâ€“persistence relationship from absorbing a separate explanatory problem.

Agency identifies viability-oriented organisational activity. Biological Evaluation concerns how differences acquire significance relative to that activity. Organised persistence concerns continuity of living organisation through change.

For the present article, Biological Evaluation matters only insofar as changing conditions can differ in their consequences for continuity and living activity can be modulated accordingly.

A perturbation that threatens viable organisation is not equivalent to a condition that leaves it unaffected. A change that opens a viable course of activity differs from one that closes it. Such differences can become biologically significant through their relation to the organisation of Agency.

But this article does not require a general theory of Biological Evaluation or biological significance.

The narrower point is sufficient:

> **Viability-oriented activity can be differentially organised in relation to conditions that matter for the continuation of living organisation.**

This helps explain how Agency can contribute to persistence under changing circumstances without making Evaluation synonymous with Agency.

## 8. Development as Continuity Through Transformation

Development provides a particularly clear illustration of organised persistence.

An organism can change dramatically while remaining the same continuing living individual relevant to the explanandum.

Structures emerge and disappear. Physiological relations change. New capacities develop. Patterns of activity are reorganised. The conditions under which viability is maintained at one developmental stage may differ substantially from those required at another.

If persistence meant preservation of a fixed state, development would present a paradox.

Under an organisational account, it does not.

The relevant continuity lies in the organised persistence of the living system through transformation.

Agency contributes to this continuity where viability-oriented activities regulate developmental change, respond to perturbation, repair disruption, or reorganise activity as conditions alter.

This does not mean that development as a whole is an expression of Agency.

Development has its own mechanisms, histories, and explanatory structures. Agency becomes relevant only where viability-oriented organisational activity makes a difference to the developmental continuity being explained.

Development therefore illustrates the central principle:

> **Continuity of living organisation can be maintained through transformation rather than despite it.**

## 9. Organismâ€“Environment Relations

Living systems do not maintain viability independently of their surroundings.

Resources, temperature, chemical conditions, other organisms, and many additional environmental relations can affect whether living organisation continues. Organisms can also alter aspects of the environments in which their activity occurs.

These relations matter to organised persistence without requiring APS to treat organism and environment as a single higher-order agent.

The relevant question remains target-specific.

For a particular persistence explanandum, which environmental relations materially affect the conditions under which the living organisation can continue? And which activities of the organism modify those relations in ways that make a difference to viability?

Agency can therefore include activity materially realised through organismâ€“environment interaction without relocating Agency automatically to a broader spatial extent.

This is also where Scale becomes relevant.

Scale asks where persistence relevant to the explanandum is organised across spatial and temporal extents. It does not identify a hierarchy of agents, nor do wider scales themselves act upon local biological processes.

Organismâ€“environment relations matter when materially realised interactions, constraints, or conditions across those extents alter the organisation whose persistence is being explained.

That is sufficient for the present argument. Whether broader ecological organisations themselves warrant Agency attribution is a separate question.

## 10. Agency Does Not Explain Persistence by Itself

The close relationship between Agency and organised persistence creates a methodological danger.

Once viability-oriented activity has been identified, it can be tempting to treat Agency as the explanation of biological continuity.

APS should not do this.

Agency is an analytic projection, not a general-purpose causal variable.

To explain a particular case of persistence, the relevant materially realised activities and relations must be identified. If repair matters, the repair mechanisms must be specified. If regulation matters, the relevant regulatory organisation must be shown. If compensatory reorganisation maintains viability, the material changes through which compensation occurs require explanation.

The statement that a system â€œexercises Agencyâ€ cannot substitute for these explanations.

Nor does every persistence explanandum require Agency to receive explanatory priority.

For some questions, a mechanistic, physiological, developmental, ecological, or other established explanation may already specify the relevant dependencies adequately. In such a case, redescribing the phenomenon in agential terms adds no explanatory gain.

The APS question is therefore comparative:

> **For this specified persistence explanandum, what does analysis under Agency explain that the strongest relevant comparator does not already explain?**

The answer can be: nothing.

Where Agency does provide explanatory gain, that gain must be demonstrated. It might clarify why particular activities count as viability-relevant rather than merely occurring, identify organisational dependencies omitted by a narrower comparator, or reveal why maintenance and re-establishment rather than fixed-state preservation are central to the explanandum.

But these are possibilities to be tested, not benefits guaranteed by applying APS terminology.

Organised persistence therefore provides an explanatory target. Agency provides one possible analytic projection through which aspects of that target can be investigated.

The relation between them is substantive without being explanatory monopoly.

## 11. Present Activity and Continuity Through Time

Agency occurs in the present.

Organised persistence necessarily extends through time.

This difference can make it seem that Agency and persistence occupy separate temporal domains. They do not.

Present viability-oriented activity is materially situated within a continuing organisation whose current state bears the effects of previous activity and whose continuation depends upon what happens now.

Regulation, repair, and reorganisation occur at particular times. Their consequences can alter whether living organisation continues beyond those moments.

Agency therefore has temporally extended consequences without itself becoming synonymous with historical persistence.

This distinction is especially important at the boundary with evolution.

The organisation through which present Agency is enacted has a history, and the conditions under which living systems persist can be transformed across generations. But historical evolutionary transformation is not simply Agency operating over a longer timescale.

The relationship between present-tense biological Agency and evolutionary explanation requires separate analysis.

For the present article, the relevant conclusion is narrower:

> **Present activity can make a material difference to continuity through time without Agency and persistence becoming the same explanatory concept.**

## 12. Why the Relationship Matters

The distinction between Agency and organised persistence prevents two opposite errors.

The first is to separate them too strongly.

If persistence is treated as passive duration, the active organisation required for living continuity can disappear from view. Regulation, repair, compensation, and reorganisation then appear as secondary features of systems whose persistence is already assumed.

APS instead asks how continuity is materially maintained and re-established through change.

The second error is to collapse them.

If Agency is defined simply as whatever produces persistence, or organised persistence is treated as the outcome of Agency, the distinction between explanatory target and analytic projection disappears. Agency becomes an abstract causal force and persistence becomes its product.

APS rejects both moves.

Agency and organised persistence concern the same living organisation under distinguishable explanatory questions.

Agency asks about viability-oriented organisational activity.

Organised persistence asks about continuity through change.

The explanatory connection between them must be established in particular cases by showing how materially realised activities affect the conditions under which that continuity is maintained or re-established.

This preserves the importance of Agency without asking it to explain more than it can.

## Conclusion

Living continuity is not passive endurance.

Living systems persist while their materials change, their structures are remodelled, their environments fluctuate, and their organisation develops, repairs, and reorganises. Persistence therefore cannot generally be identified with preservation of a fixed state.

APS describes this continuity as **organised persistence**.

Biological Agency addresses the same living organisation from another analytic perspective:

> **Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity.**

The relationship is neither identity nor causal succession.

Agency does not first create viability and thereby produce persistence. Organised persistence is not an independent outcome generated by Agency. Both concern one viability-oriented, constraint-closed living organisation.

Yet the distinction is explanatory rather than merely terminological. Activities analysed under Agency can make a material difference to whether conditions of viable continuity are maintained or re-established. Regulation can counter perturbation. Repair can restore organisation. Compensation can preserve functioning under disruption. Reorganisation can enable continuity when previous arrangements no longer suffice.

Such activity can therefore contribute to organised persistence without becoming its complete or sufficient explanation.

The central APS claim is consequently precise:

> **Agency identifies viability-oriented organisational activity in the present; organised persistence identifies the continuity of living organisation through change. Their explanatory relationship is established where materially realised activities contribute to maintaining or re-establishing the conditions of that continuity.**

Whether this perspective provides explanatory gain remains target- and comparator-relative.

Agency matters to organised persistence not because it stands outside living organisation and causes continuity, but because living continuity can depend upon what living organisation does.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

What is the explanatory relationship between present-tense viability-oriented Agency and the organised persistence of living organisation through change?

### Architectural Role

This article is an Extension article within the Conceptual Foundations cluster.

It extends the canonical APS account of Agency by examining how viability-oriented organisational activity relates to continuity through change without treating Agency and organised persistence as successive stages, independent causes, or separate components of Life.

### Relationship to the Agency Anchor

**Biological Agency as the Activity of Self-Maintenance** establishes the canonical definition of biological Agency and the conditions governing Agency attribution.

The present article does not redefine Agency or supply an alternative attribution criterion.

It asks what explanatory relationship follows once Agency is considered in relation to the continuity of living organisation.

### Relationship to Organised Persistence

Organised persistence is an explanatory target concerned with continuity of living organisation through change.

Agency is an analytic projection concerned with viability-oriented organisational activity.

Activities analysed under Agency can contribute materially to maintaining and re-establishing conditions of organised persistence, but Agency is neither an independent cause nor a sufficient explanation of that persistence.

### Relationship to Process

Process asks how continuity is maintained despite change.

This article therefore approaches a question closely related to Process, but from within the Agency corpus: what difference does viability-oriented organisational activity make to that continuity?

Agency and Process remain analytic projections of the same living organisation rather than independent explanatory systems.

### Relationship to Scale

Scale asks where persistence relevant to an explanandum is organised across spatial and temporal extents.

Agency attribution does not follow from spatial extent, and wider scales do not themselves act upon living systems. Relations across extents matter where materially realised constraints, interactions, or conditions alter the organisation whose persistence is being explained.

### Relationship to Biological Evaluation

Biological Evaluation is the process through which Agency generates significance.

It is not synonymous with Agency. This article invokes Biological Evaluation only to clarify how changing conditions can matter differently relative to viability and thereby participate in the modulation of activity relevant to continuity.

The positive theory of Biological Evaluation belongs elsewhere in the APS corpus.

### Evolutionary Boundary

Present forms of Agency are enacted within historically formed living organisation, but evolution is not Agency extended across a longer timescale.

The relationship between present-tense Agency and historical evolutionary transformation belongs to **Biological Agency, Evolution, and the Architecture of Biological Explanation** and is not developed here.

### Explanatory-Gain Condition

Agency terminology does not automatically improve an explanation of persistence.

For any specified explanandum, APS must compare the Agency analysis with the strongest relevant comparator and identify what additional dependency, distinction, or organisational relation the Agency analysis explains.

If the comparator already explains the target adequately, the explanatory-gain verdict can be null.

### Corpus Significance

This article establishes the APS relationship between Agency and organised persistence without converting that relationship into a causal pipeline.

Its distinctive claim is:

> **Agency and organised persistence are analytically distinguishable aspects of one living organisation: Agency identifies viability-oriented organisational activity in the present, while organised persistence identifies continuity through change. Their explanatory relationship depends upon materially realised activities making a difference to the maintenance or re-establishment of that continuity.**

## Introduction

The paper *Agency as the Defining Activity of Life: A Viability-Oriented Framework Integrating Process and Scale*, published in *Biological Theory*, began from a familiar but difficult biological question: what distinguishes a living system from a nonliving one?

Rather than beginning with a list of characteristic structures or capacities, the paper focused on activity. Living systems regulate internal conditions, maintain boundaries, repair damage, reorganise in response to disturbance, and continually contribute to conditions under which their organisation can continue. The paper called this viability-oriented activity **biological Agency** and proposed it as the **defining activity of Life** (Spencer 2026).

That formulation remains important, but it raises a question that subsequent development of APS makes possible to state more precisely. If Life is **viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation**, and biological agency is **viability-oriented organisational activity**, in what sense can Agency still be described as the defining activity of Life?

The answer requires distinguishing two closely related questions:

**What is Life?**

and

**What is distinctive about the activity of living organisation?**

APS does not now give these questions the same answer. Life identifies a form of organisation. Agency identifies what that organisation does in relation to viability. The distinction does not diminish the importance of Agency. It clarifies why Agency can be the defining activity of Life without being the complete definition of Life.

## Where This Article Fits

This article is a clarification of the Agency thesis first developed in the published *Biological Theory* paper. Its purpose is not to provide the general APS account of biological Agency. That role belongs to **Biological Agency as the Activity of Self-Maintenance**, the Anchor article for the APS Agency corpus.

The present article addresses a narrower question: **what does it mean to call Agency the defining activity of Life?**

Answering that question requires representing the published thesis accurately while distinguishing it from the subsequently clarified APS architecture. The original paper gave Agency a particularly strong theoretical role. Current APS retains its central insight while distinguishing more carefully between Life as viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation and Agency as the viability-oriented organisational activity of that living organisation.

This article therefore connects a fixed published stage in the development of APS with the framework's current formulation. It does not independently redefine Agency, provide criteria for agency attribution, develop the full relationship between Agency and organised persistence, or compare APS with contemporary theories of biological agency. Those questions are addressed elsewhere in the Agency corpus.

Its concern is one claim: **Agency can remain the defining activity of Life without Agency becoming the definition of Life itself.**

## 1. The Published Agency Thesis

The published paper approached Life through what living systems do.

Cells and organisms undergo continual material and organisational change. Components are produced, transformed, damaged, repaired, and replaced. Internal conditions fluctuate. Environmental circumstances change. Yet living systems can maintain a form of organised continuity through these transformations.

The paper argued that this persistence is not adequately characterised as passive endurance. Living systems actively contribute to maintaining and re-establishing conditions compatible with their continued existence. Regulation, repair, boundary maintenance, responsiveness, and reorganisation are biologically diverse activities, but they can all bear upon the viability of the system performing them.

The paper used **Agency** to bring this activity into explanatory focus. Agency did not mean consciousness, intelligence, deliberate choice, or human-like intention. It referred to viability-oriented activity through which living systems sustain and reconstitute their organisation across time and changing conditions (Spencer 2026).

That was the sense in which Agency was proposed as the defining activity of Life.

The claim was deliberately stronger than the observation that organisms happen to regulate themselves. It proposed that active contribution to the conditions of continued viability is fundamental to the kind of organisation characteristic of living systems. A rock can persist without acting to maintain the conditions under which it remains a rock. Living systems persist differently: their continuation depends upon organised activity through which conditions relevant to their viability are continually maintained, restored, or altered.

The paper therefore shifted attention from a catalogue of what living systems possess to the organisation of what living systems do.

It also sought to make this proposal empirically tractable. The paper proposed biosignatures including homeostasis, adaptive plasticity, selective boundary regulation, goal-directed behaviour, recursive self-repair, and cross-scale coordination as possible indicators of viability-oriented activity, while acknowledging unresolved questions about thresholds, borderline cases, and nonliving self-organisation (Spencer 2026).

The published proposal should be understood in that context. It was not an attempt to introduce Agency as an additional causal force alongside metabolism, physiology, development, or molecular regulation. It sought to redescribe established biological activity in relation to the organisational conditions under which living systems continue to exist.

Its central thesis can therefore be stated simply:

**Living systems do not merely persist. They actively contribute to maintaining and re-establishing conditions compatible with their own continued viability.**

The paper called that activity biological Agency.

## 2. Defining Life and Identifying Its Defining Activity

The phrase **defining activity of Life** can be misunderstood if defining *Life* and identifying the characteristic *activity of living organisation* are treated as the same task.

APS now distinguishes them.

**Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation.**

This is the canonical APS definition of Life. It identifies living organisation in terms of the relation between viability and constraint closure rather than by reducing Life to a list of traits or to any single activity.

**Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity.**

Agency therefore answers a different question. It asks what living organisation does in relation to conditions relevant to its continued functioning.

The distinction can be expressed compactly:

> **Life identifies the organisation. Agency identifies its viability-oriented activity.**

This does not divide biological reality into a living organisation on one side and an independent thing called Agency on the other. Agency exists only as activity of materially realised living organisation. Conversely, living organisation is not a static arrangement that merely possesses Agency as an optional property. Its continuation depends upon ongoing activity.

Agency is therefore an **analytic projection** of living organisation rather than an additional component or cause within it.

This distinction resolves an ambiguity that arises if Agency is asked simultaneously to answer what Life *is* and what living systems *do*. If Agency is defined through the activity of living systems and Life is then defined solely through Agency, the two concepts risk becoming circular. Distinguishing organisation from activity gives each concept a clearer explanatory role.

The result does not require abandoning the title of the published paper.

Agency can be **the defining activity of Life** because viability-oriented organisational activity characterises the active enactment of living organisation without Agency having to provide the complete definition of that organisation.

## 3. Why Agency Remains Defining

Calling Agency *defining* makes a stronger claim than saying that living systems exhibit activity.

All physical systems undergo change, and many nonliving systems participate in complex causal processes. Biological Agency cannot therefore be identified simply with activity, change, causation, responsiveness, or complexity.

The relevant activity is **viability-oriented organisational activity**.

Viability introduces an asymmetry among conditions. Some changes contribute to maintaining or re-establishing conditions under which the organisation can continue functioning; others impair or destroy those conditions. Agency concerns activity organised relative to this difference.

This is why repair is biologically significant in a way that arbitrary molecular change is not. It is why regulation can be analysed in relation to conditions of continued functioning rather than merely as one causal sequence among others. It is also why biological Agency need not imply conscious evaluation. The relevant asymmetry is grounded in the viability of the living organisation.

Constraint closure adds a further organisational condition. Living systems depend upon constraints that regulate processes while themselves being generated, maintained, or re-established through the organisation in which they operate. Agency occurs within this viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation; it does not substitute for it.

The claim that Agency is defining should therefore not be read as:

> Life = Agency.

Nor should it be read as:

> Agency is the fundamental causal force producing living organisation.

The defensible claim is more precise:

> **Living organisation is distinctive in part because its continuing organisation is enacted through viability-oriented organisational activity. Agency is the APS analytic projection that brings this activity into explanatory focus.**

That is sufficient for Agency to remain the defining **activity** of Life.

## 4. Agency and Organised Persistence

The original Agency thesis was closely connected to persistence. Living systems continually undergo change while maintaining forms of organised continuity, and the published paper emphasised that such persistence is an ongoing achievement rather than passive endurance (Spencer 2026).

That insight remains.

What requires clarification is the relationship between Agency and the phenomenon being explained.

**Organised persistence** is the continuity of living organisation through change. Components turn over, internal states fluctuate, damage occurs, development alters organisation, and environmental conditions vary. Yet living organisation can continue through these transformations.

Agency contributes to explaining that persistence because living systems engage in viability-oriented organisational activity. Repair, regulation, reorganisation, boundary maintenance, and other activities can materially contribute to maintaining or re-establishing conditions under which living organisation continues.

But organised persistence should not therefore be treated as an output generated by Agency alone.

The full explanation of a particular case may require mechanisms, constraints, temporal relations, environmental conditions, developmental histories, evolutionary histories, or other materially realised dependencies. Agency identifies one explanatory question within that organisation: how does the activity of the living system bear upon viability?

The more detailed relationship between Agency and organised persistence belongs to **Agency and Organised Persistence**. The important point here is narrower. Describing Agency as the defining activity of Life does not make Agency the sole cause or complete explanation of living persistence.

It identifies the characteristic viability-oriented activity through which living organisation participates in maintaining and re-establishing conditions of its continuation.

## 5. Agency within the APS Architecture

The published paper brought Agency, Process, and Scale together within a common framework. Subsequent development has clarified how these terms should be related.

They are not a sequence:

> Agency â†’ Process â†’ Scale

They are not independent components of Life, and they are not levels of biological organisation.

**Agency, Process, and Scale are analytic projections of one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation.**

Agency asks **what living systems do**: it brings viability-oriented organisational activity into explanatory focus.

Process asks **how continuity is maintained despite change**.

Scale asks **where persistence relevant to an explanandum is organised across spatial and temporal extents**.

The distinctions are analytic, but they concern materially realised biological organisation. They allow different explanatory questions to be directed towards the same living system without turning those questions into separate entities or causes.

This matters for the defining-activity thesis because Agency need not be made foundational to Process and Scale in order to remain biologically fundamental. Calling Agency the defining activity of Life does not mean that every biological explanation must begin with Agency or ultimately reduce to it.

It means that when the explanatory question concerns what living organisation does in relation to its viability, Agency identifies the relevant analytic projection.

The published thesis can therefore be retained without an Agency-first architecture.

## 6. What the Original Thesis Establishes

The clarification developed here allows the surviving content of the original thesis to be stated without either weakening it into a trivial observation or asking it to establish more than it can support.

The first claim is that **living organisation is active**. Living systems continually participate in maintaining and re-establishing conditions relevant to their own viability.

The second is that this activity is **viability-oriented**. Biological changes are not equivalent with respect to the continuation of the living organisation.

The third is that this activity does not require **conscious intention, deliberation, intelligence, or cognition**. Those capacities may occur in some forms of life, but they are not constitutive of biological Agency.

The fourth is that Agency is **organisational rather than an additional causal force**. An agential analysis does not replace the molecular, physiological, developmental, ecological, or other mechanisms through which biological activity is materially realised.

The fifth is that calling Agency the defining activity of Life does **not** establish that Agency provides explanatory gain for every biological explanandum. A warranted Agency analysis and a demonstrated explanatory contribution are different claims. Where explanatory gain is claimed, it must be assessed relative to the specified target and the strongest relevant comparator.

The original paper's central insight can therefore survive while its explanatory burden becomes more precisely bounded.

## 7. Why the Title Still Holds

The question with which this article began can now be answered directly.

If Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation, why call Agency the defining activity of Life?

Because living organisation is not merely a configuration that happens to endure. Its continuation is continually enacted through activity occurring in relation to conditions of viability. Biological Agency names that viability-oriented organisational activity.

The distinction between Life and Agency therefore does not separate two independent biological realities.

**Life identifies the organisation.**

**Agency identifies what that living organisation does in relation to viability.**

The published paper was right to make this activity central. What subsequent clarification adds is a more exact account of the theoretical work the concept should perform.

Agency does not need to define the whole of Life in order to identify its defining activity. It does not need to generate organised persistence by itself. It does not need to stand above Process or Scale. And it does not need to replace established biological mechanisms or explanations.

Its role is both narrower and clearer:

> **Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity. It is the defining activity of Life because living organisation is continually enacted through activity that maintains and re-establishes conditions relevant to its own viability.**

That is the strongest continuing interpretation of the original Agency thesis.

## Conclusion

*Agency as the Defining Activity of Life* proposed that understanding living systems requires attention not only to what they contain or which traits they display, but to the activity through which they contribute to maintaining the conditions of their own continued existence.

That central insight remains part of APS.

The developed framework now distinguishes the organisational definition of Life from the activity of living organisation:

> **Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation.**

> **Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity.**

These formulations answer related but different questions. The first identifies the organisation characteristic of Life. The second identifies its viability-oriented activity.

Organised persistence, meanwhile, identifies a phenomenon requiring explanation: the continuity of living organisation despite material, environmental, and organisational change. Agency can contribute to such explanations without becoming their sole cause or sufficient explanation.

Agency, Process, and Scale likewise need not form an Agency-first sequence. They are analytic projections of one living organisation rather than components of biological reality.

The title of the published paper can therefore be retained in a precise sense. Agency is not the complete definition of Life. It is the defining activity of Life because viability-oriented organisational activity is characteristic of how living organisation continually maintains and re-establishes conditions of its own continuation.

The distinction preserves the central Agency thesis while making clear what Agency identifies, what it does not replace, and what further work is required whenever an Agency analysis claims explanatory gain.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

In what precise sense can biological Agency be described as the defining activity of Life when Life itself is defined as viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation?

### Architectural Role

This article is a Clarification article within the Conceptual Foundations cluster.

Its function is to interpret and delimit the thesis first developed in *Agency as the Defining Activity of Life: A Viability-Oriented Framework Integrating Process and Scale* (Spencer 2026).

The article distinguishes the definition of Life from the identification of its defining activity. Life identifies viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation; Agency identifies the viability-oriented organisational activity of that living organisation.

### Relationship to the Agency Anchor

**Biological Agency as the Activity of Self-Maintenance** is the canonical Agency Anchor. It establishes what biological Agency is, the conditions governing its attribution, its distinction from explanatory Scale, and the difference between warranted Agency attribution and demonstrated explanatory gain.

The present article does not duplicate those functions.

It asks instead why Agency, once defined and bounded by the Anchor, can properly be described as the defining activity of Life.

### Relationship to Organised Persistence

Organised persistence is principally a phenomenon requiring explanation rather than an outcome produced by Agency alone.

Agency can contribute to explanations of organised persistence by identifying viability-oriented organisational activity involved in maintaining or re-establishing conditions of continuation. The detailed relationship between these concepts is developed in **Agency and Organised Persistence**.

### Position within APS

Agency, Process, and Scale are analytic projections of one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation rather than independent causes, components, stages, dimensions, or levels of biological reality.

Calling Agency the defining activity of Life therefore gives Agency neither hierarchical priority nor universal explanatory priority. It identifies the characteristic viability-oriented activity of living organisation.

### Corpus Significance

This article preserves the interpretive connection between the published *Biological Theory* Agency thesis and the developed APS framework without retrospectively rewriting the published paper.

Its distinctive contribution is the proposition:

> **Agency can be the defining activity of Life without being the definition of Life.**

For the canonical operational account of biological Agency, see **Biological Agency as the Activity of Self-Maintenance**. For the detailed relationship between Agency and organised persistence, see **Agency and Organised Persistence**. For the boundary between biological Agency and intention, cognition, and representation, see **Biological Agency Without Intentions**.

## Introduction

Living systems have histories.

The organisation through which an organism regulates its activity, repairs damage, develops, reproduces, and interacts with its surroundings did not arise independently of evolutionary history. Contemporary organisms inherit structures, capacities, constraints, and developmental relations shaped through processes extending across generations.

Yet living systems also act in the present.

They maintain and re-establish conditions of viability through materially realised activity occurring now. APS describes this as **biological Agency: viability-oriented organisational activity** (Spencer 2026).

The relationship between these two explanatory perspectives requires care. An evolutionary history can help explain why a present organisation exists in the form that it does, but it does not thereby explain every aspect of how that organisation currently operates. Conversely, explaining present-tense Agency does not by itself explain the historical processes through which the relevant organisation arose or changed.

The central question is therefore:

> **How does present-tense biological Agency relate to historical evolutionary transformation without Agency becoming an evolutionary mechanism, evolution becoming Agency extended through time, or either explanation displacing the other?**

APS distinguishes three questions that can otherwise easily be conflated:

1. **Historical dependence:** how is present Agency conditioned by organisation with an evolutionary history?
2. **Evolutionary consequence:** when can materially realised agential activity alter conditions relevant to evolutionary outcomes?
3. **Explanatory gain:** when does analysing such activity explicitly under Agency improve explanation of a specified evolutionary explanandum?

These questions are related, but they are not equivalent.

## Where This Article Fits

This article examines the explanatory interface between biological Agency and evolution.

It does not redefine biological Agency. **Biological Agency as the Activity of Self-Maintenance** establishes the canonical APS account of Agency and the conditions governing its attribution.

Nor does this article establish why Agency is the defining activity of Life, why Agency does not require intention or cognition, or how Agency relates to organised persistence within the lifetime of a living system. Those questions belong to earlier articles in the Agency corpus.

The present article begins from those results and asks what follows when present-tense viability-oriented activity is considered in relation to evolutionary history.

Its scope is deliberately narrower than a general APS account of evolution. Questions concerning what evolves, lineage continuity, phylogenetic organisation, taxonomy, and the historical transformation of organised persistence belong to the APS treatment of evolution itself.

Here the focus remains on **Agency**.

The article therefore distinguishes the evolutionary history of the organisation through which Agency is enacted from the possible evolutionary consequences of agential activity and from the further question of whether explicit Agency analysis provides explanatory gain.

This prevents present activity and historical transformation from being separated completely while also preventing them from being collapsed into a single explanatory process.

## 1. Present Organisation and Evolutionary History

Every living organism exists through an organisation with a history.

Metabolic pathways, physiological regulatory systems, developmental architectures, sensory capacities, patterns of behaviour, reproductive systems, and organismâ€“environment relations can all depend upon inherited organisation transformed through evolutionary processes.

Present Agency is therefore historically conditioned.

But historical dependence does not mean that evolutionary history provides a complete explanation of present activity.

Consider a regulatory capacity that currently contributes to maintaining viable physiological conditions. Its evolutionary history may help explain why the relevant structures and capacities exist. A present-tense physiological explanation may identify the mechanisms through which regulation occurs. An Agency analysis may ask how that activity is organised relative to conditions bearing upon the viability of the living system.

These explanations need not compete merely because they concern the same biological phenomenon.

They can address different dependencies.

This gives the first distinction required by the Agencyâ€“evolution interface:

> **The evolutionary history of an organisation and the present activity enacted through that organisation are distinguishable explanatory targets.**

Evolutionary history can condition the possibilities of present Agency without replacing an explanation of what the living system is currently doing.

Likewise, present Agency can depend upon historically formed organisation without becoming an explanation of its own evolutionary origin.

## 2. Historical Orientation: Organisation and Evolution

The distinction has deep roots in biological thought.

Aristotle investigated organisms as organised living beings whose parts and activities were intelligible in relation to the life of the whole organism. Darwin transformed biological explanation by providing a historical account of evolutionary change and adaptation without requiring external design.

These traditions should not be mapped directly onto APS.

Aristotle is not the historical representative of Agency, and Darwinian evolution is not the APS Process projection. Nor does contemporary biology add Scale as a third stage completing a historical sequence.

Their relevance here is more limited.

They illustrate a persistent distinction between questions about **how living organisation operates** and questions about **how biological organisation has been historically transformed**.

Darwinian explanation also changed the status of purposive language in biology. Adaptive organisation could be explained historically without supposing that organisms or an external designer consciously intended the resulting form.

APS accepts that achievement.

Its account of Agency does not restore intentional design to biology. Biological Agency does not require conscious purpose, and present viability-oriented activity should not be substituted for evolutionary explanations of adaptation.

The remaining question is how historically formed organisation can itself instantiate present-tense activity organised relative to viability.

That is the problem addressed here.

## 3. Historical Dependence

Present Agency depends upon materially realised organisation.

That organisation includes structures, processes, constraints, developmental relations, and capacities whose present forms can be historically conditioned.

This dependence matters because living systems do not begin each generation organisationally unconstrained. They inherit biological arrangements that shape what forms of activity are possible, how development proceeds, how physiological regulation occurs, and how organisms can interact with their surroundings.

Agency is enacted through this inherited and developing organisation.

But the phrase **historical dependence** must not be interpreted as a claim that evolution acts as a continuing external cause of every present agential event.

The immediate causes of a physiological adjustment, behavioural response, repair process, or developmental transition may be entirely present-tense and materially local.

Evolutionary history becomes explanatorily relevant when the question concerns why the organisation enabling those activities has the form, capacities, or dependencies that it does.

Historical and present-tense explanations can therefore intersect without becoming interchangeable.

A complete account of a particular phenomenon may sometimes require both. In other cases, one may be sufficient for the explanandum being investigated.

APS does not decide that question in advance.

## 4. Evolutionary Consequence

The explanatory relation also runs in another sense.

What organisms do can sometimes make a difference to conditions relevant to evolutionary outcomes. Work on niche construction and the extended evolutionary synthesis has emphasised ways in which organismal activity, development, and organismâ€“environment relations can modify circumstances entering evolutionary processes (Odling-Smee, Laland, and Feldman 2003; Laland et al. 2015).

Organisms move, regulate development, alter resource use, modify aspects of their environments, reproduce differentially, interact with other organisms, and change circumstances under which developmental and reproductive processes occur.

Where such activities are instances of viability-oriented organisational activity, they may appropriately be analysed under Agency.

Some of those activities can also have consequences extending beyond their immediate contribution to present viability.

They may alter exposure to environmental conditions, patterns of reproduction, developmental outcomes, ecological relations, or other materially realised circumstances relevant to evolutionary change.

But this does **not** establish Agency as an evolutionary mechanism.

To say that Agency has an evolutionary consequence is only the beginning of an explanation.

The relevant activity must be specified. The material pathway through which it affects an evolutionary dependency must be identified. The historical outcome must be connected to established evolutionary processes appropriate to the explanandum.

The methodological rule is therefore:

> **Where agential activity makes an evolutionary difference, the materially realised activity and the evolutionary dependency through which that difference occurs must be specified.**

â€œAgency affects evolutionâ€ is not by itself an evolutionary explanation.

## 5. Agency Is Not an Additional Evolutionary Mechanism

Contemporary organism-centred approaches have argued that organismal activity can participate causally in evolutionary processes rather than being treated only as an outcome of selection (Walsh 2015).

APS can recognise this contribution without treating Agency itself as an additional causal force.

An organism's activity can alter conditions relevant to selection, reproduction, development, inheritance, ecological interaction, or other processes involved in evolutionary explanations. But the causal work in such cases is performed through materially realised activities and relations.

Agency does not enter the explanation as another mechanism alongside them.

Suppose an organism modifies its environment in a way that changes conditions encountered by itself or its descendants. An Agency analysis may clarify how the relevant activity is organised relative to the organism's viability. An evolutionary explanation may then establish whether and how the resulting environmental modification affects a historical outcome.

Those explanatory contributions should not be collapsed.

The first concerns the organisational character of present activity.

The second concerns the dependencies producing evolutionary change.

Agency can therefore become relevant to an evolutionary explanation without becoming an independent evolutionary mechanism.

This distinction protects APS from turning a useful analytic projection into an unspecified causal variable.

## 6. Evolution Is Not Agency Extended Through Time

The converse error must also be avoided.

Evolution should not be understood simply as Agency operating over longer periods.

Agency concerns viability-oriented organisational activity enacted by living systems in the present.

Evolutionary transformation concerns historical change across generations through materially realised processes and relations appropriate to evolutionary explananda.

Present activity can contribute to historical outcomes, but the existence of that contribution does not erase the distinction between the two.

Nor does organised persistence erase it.

Living systems maintain continuity through change during their lives. Historically extended biological continuities can also become relevant to evolutionary explanation. But this does not mean that organismal Agency simply expands through time until it becomes evolutionary Process.

The relevant question must instead be specified for the explanandum:

> **What organisation persists across the temporal extent relevant to the evolutionary question, through which materially realised relations is that continuity maintained, and how is it transformed?**

This question belongs primarily to the broader APS treatment of evolution.

Its importance here is negative but essential: historically extended continuity does not convert evolution into a temporally enlarged form of Agency.

## 7. Agency and Process

Agency and Process are complementary analytic projections of one living organisation.

Agency asks what living systems do.

Process asks how continuity is maintained despite change.

Evolution should not be identified with Process merely because evolution involves change through time.

Evolutionary theory addresses historical transformation through evolutionary mechanisms, relations, and dependencies. Process, by contrast, identifies an APS explanatory question concerning continuity through change.

The two can intersect.

For example, an evolutionary explanandum may concern the historical transformation of an organisation whose continuity across generations must itself be specified. Process questions may then become relevant to understanding the continuity being transformed.

But this does not make evolution the Process component of APS.

Nor does Process supply an alternative evolutionary theory.

The distinction matters because otherwise a methodological projection becomes confused with the biological phenomena and mechanisms being explained.

## 8. Agency and Scale

Evolutionary questions frequently extend beyond the spatial and temporal extent of an individual organism.

This does not require a hierarchy of explanatory levels.

Scale asks:

> **Where is persistence relevant to the explanandum organised across spatial and temporal extents?**

For some evolutionary questions, relevant dependencies may extend across organisms, generations, populations, developmental histories, ecological relations, or inherited environmental conditions.

These extents matter only through materially realised relations.

A wider scale does not act upon an organism. A lineage does not become an agent merely because its history extends beyond individual lifetimes. Nor does the presence of organismal Agency establish Agency at every broader extent involved in evolutionary explanation.

The task is instead to identify which relations across spatial and temporal extents make a difference to the evolutionary explanandum.

Scale therefore helps prevent a common conflation.

The temporal extension of an evolutionary process does not make it a larger form of Agency, just as the participation of many organisms in a historical process does not automatically create a higher-order agent.

## 9. From Present Activity to Historical Consequence

The Agencyâ€“evolution relationship can now be stated more precisely.

A present activity may be:

1. enacted through organisation with an evolutionary history;
2. viability-oriented for the organism in which it occurs;
3. materially consequential for conditions relevant to an evolutionary outcome; and
4. connected through specified evolutionary dependencies to historical transformation.

These propositions must be established separately.

The first concerns **historical dependence**.

The second concerns **Agency**.

The third establishes a possible **evolutionary consequence**.

The fourth belongs to the **evolutionary explanation** itself.

None follows automatically from the others.

A trait can have an evolutionary history without every present use of that trait being explanatorily important to evolution.

An activity can qualify as biological Agency without having significant evolutionary consequences.

An activity can alter an evolutionary condition without Agency terminology improving the evolutionary explanation.

And an evolutionary explanation can be adequate without explicitly invoking Agency.

The distinctions are therefore methodological safeguards against explanatory inflation.

## 10. Organised Persistence Across Different Temporal Questions

The APS account of Agency and organised persistence establishes that they are analytically distinguishable aspects of one living organisation.

That result should not be extrapolated without qualification into evolutionary history.

Within an organismal explanandum, organised persistence may concern continuity of living organisation through regulation, repair, development, and reorganisation.

An evolutionary explanandum may involve a different temporal extent and a different bearer of relevant continuity.

The question of what persists must therefore be determined by the explanandum rather than assumed from the presence of organismal Agency.

This is especially important because biological continuity can be organised through relations that extend beyond the lifetime of one organism.

Inheritance, reproduction, developmental recurrence, population processes, ecological relations, and lineage histories can all become relevant depending upon the evolutionary target.

But their relevance does not imply that all such organisation constitutes Agency.

Agency attribution and the identification of historically relevant continuity remain separate questions.

The Agencyâ€“evolution interface therefore requires attention to continuity without indiscriminate extension of agency attribution.

## 11. Explanatory Gain

The presence of Agency in an evolutionary context does not guarantee that Agency provides explanatory gain.

Suppose a well-established evolutionary explanation already specifies the variation, inheritance, developmental relations, ecological conditions, reproductive differences, and historical dependencies relevant to an explanandum.

Adding the statement that the organisms involved are agents may contribute nothing.

APS must permit that result.

The relevant comparative question is:

> **For this specified evolutionary explanandum, what does explicit analysis under Agency explain that the strongest relevant evolutionary comparator does not already explain?**

Several outcomes are possible.

Agency analysis might identify a viability-relative dependency that the comparator leaves implicit. It might show why particular present activities systematically alter conditions entering an evolutionary process. It might clarify a relationship between organismal activity and historical transformation that would otherwise remain underdescribed.

Alternatively, the established comparator may already explain all relevant dependencies.

In that case, the explanatory-gain verdict is null.

APS should not respond by redescribing the same mechanism in agential language and treating the redescription as additional explanation.

Explanatory gain must be demonstrated at the matched target.

## 12. Historical Dependence, Evolutionary Consequence, and Explanatory Gain

The architecture of the Agencyâ€“evolution relationship can therefore be expressed through three distinctions.

### Historical Dependence

Present Agency is enacted through living organisation whose structures, capacities, constraints, and relations have evolutionary histories.

This establishes historical conditioning.

It does not make evolutionary history a complete explanation of present Agency.

### Evolutionary Consequence

Some materially realised agential activities can alter conditions relevant to evolutionary outcomes.

This establishes a possible connection between present activity and historical transformation.

It does not make Agency an independent evolutionary mechanism.

### Explanatory Gain

Explicit Agency analysis contributes to an evolutionary explanation only when it identifies something explanatorily relevant that the strongest matched comparator does not already explain.

This establishes methodological significance.

It cannot be inferred merely from historical dependence or evolutionary consequence.

Together these distinctions allow APS to connect present organisation with evolutionary history without collapsing them.

## 13. The Architecture of Biological Explanation

Biological phenomena frequently support more than one legitimate explanatory question.

A present biological organisation can have a history.

A historically formed capacity can be active now.

Present activity can alter conditions with future consequences.

Historical transformation can change the organisation through which future activity occurs.

None of this requires those explanations to become one undifferentiated account.

APS treats Agency, Process, and Scale as **analytic projections rather than components of reality**.

Agency concerns what living systems do.

Process concerns how continuity is maintained despite change.

Scale concerns where persistence relevant to an explanandum is organised across spatial and temporal extents.

Evolutionary explanations can intersect with all three questions without being reducible to any one of them.

This is the relevant architecture.

It is not a historical progression from Aristotle through Darwin to APS. It is not a hierarchy in which present organisation occupies one level and evolution another. And it is not a causal sequence in which Agency generates persistence and persistence subsequently becomes evolution.

Instead, the explanatory task is to identify the target, specify the relevant material dependencies, distinguish present activity from historical transformation, and determine whether relating them provides explanatory gain.

## Conclusion

Living systems are simultaneously historical and active in the present.

The organisation through which biological Agency is enacted has an evolutionary history. Present viability-oriented activity can also alter materially realised conditions that sometimes matter to evolutionary outcomes.

These facts establish an important relationship between Agency and evolution, but they do not erase their explanatory differences.

Biological Agency is not an additional evolutionary mechanism.

Evolution is not Agency extended across generations.

Historical dependence does not by itself establish evolutionary consequence, and evolutionary consequence does not by itself establish explanatory gain.

The relationship must instead be reconstructed for particular explananda.

Present Agency can be historically conditioned by inherited organisation. Agential activity can sometimes alter conditions entering evolutionary processes. Where it does, the material pathway connecting activity to historical consequence must be specified. And where Agency is proposed as explanatorily useful, its contribution must be assessed against the strongest relevant evolutionary comparator.

The resulting position is deliberately bounded:

> **Present-tense Agency and historical evolutionary transformation address distinguishable but potentially related explanatory dependencies. Biological Agency is enacted through living organisation with an evolutionary history, and materially realised agential activities can sometimes alter conditions relevant to evolutionary outcomes. Neither fact makes Agency an independent evolutionary mechanism or evolution a temporally extended form of Agency. Their explanatory relationship must be established for a specified explanandum through the material dependencies connecting present activity with historical transformation.**

This is how APS relates Agency and evolution without subordinating one to the other.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

How does present-tense biological Agency relate to historical evolutionary transformation without Agency becoming an evolutionary mechanism, evolution becoming Agency extended through time, or either explanation displacing the other?

### Architectural Role

This article occupies the Agencyâ€“evolution interface within APS.

It does not provide a general theory of evolution and does not redefine Agency. Its function is to distinguish the historical conditioning of present Agency, the possible evolutionary consequences of materially realised agential activity, and the explanatory contribution Agency analysis can make to specified evolutionary explananda.

### Historical Dependence

Present Agency is enacted through living organisation whose structures, capacities, constraints, and relations can have evolutionary histories.

Historical dependence does not make evolutionary history a complete explanation of present activity.

### Evolutionary Consequence

Materially realised activities analysed under Agency can sometimes alter conditions relevant to evolutionary outcomes.

Such consequences must be connected to specified evolutionary dependencies. Agency itself is not an additional evolutionary mechanism.

### Relationship to Process

Process asks how continuity is maintained despite change.

Evolution involves historical transformation but is not therefore identical with the APS Process projection. Process questions can become relevant to evolutionary explananda where continuity through transformation requires explanation.

### Relationship to Scale

Scale asks where persistence relevant to an explanandum is organised across spatial and temporal extents.

Evolutionary explanation can involve relations extending across organisms and generations without those wider extents becoming higher-order agents or causally acting scales.

### Relationship to Organised Persistence

Agency and organised persistence remain analytically distinguishable.

When evolutionary questions concern historically extended continuity, the organisation whose persistence is relevant must be identified for the specified explanandum. It cannot simply be extrapolated from organismal Agency.

### Evolutionary-Theory Boundary

Questions concerning what evolves, lineage continuity, phylogenetic organisation, taxonomy, and the general historical transformation of organised persistence belong to the APS treatment of evolution rather than to this article.

This article remains focused on the explanatory relevance of present-tense Agency to evolutionary questions.

### Explanatory-Gain Condition

The presence of agential activity does not establish explanatory gain.

For a specified evolutionary explanandum, Agency analysis must be compared with the strongest relevant evolutionary explanation. If the comparator already explains the relevant dependencies adequately, the Agency contribution can be null.

### Corpus Significance

This article establishes a three-part control for the APS Agency corpus:

> **historical dependence â†’ evolutionary consequence â†’ explanatory gain**

The three must not be conflated.

Present Agency can depend upon historically formed organisation without evolutionary history replacing present-tense explanation. Agential activity can have evolutionary consequences without Agency becoming an evolutionary mechanism. And neither relationship establishes explanatory gain unless Agency contributes something to the specified explanandum beyond the strongest relevant comparator.
