## Introduction: The Problem of Human Values

Human values are among the most influential features of collective life. They shape individual decisions, organise social relationships, influence political institutions, and guide the formation of moral systems. Across cultures and throughout history, values have informed what people regard as desirable, worthwhile, just, or worthy of protection. Yet despite their importance, there is no broadly accepted account of what human values are or how they should be understood within the natural world.

Different disciplines approach values from different perspectives. Psychology often treats values as relatively enduring individual preferences or motivational orientations. Sociology examines how values organise social relationships and institutions. Anthropology investigates the diversity of value systems across cultures, while philosophy asks whether values are objective, subjective, or culturally constructed. Biology has traditionally contributed comparatively little to this discussion, largely because values are often regarded as belonging to the domains of culture, morality, or rational reflection rather than to the organisation of living systems themselves.

These disciplinary perspectives have produced important insights, but they also leave a significant explanatory gap. They describe how values function within particular domains without providing a unified account of why values arise in the first place or how they relate to the organisation of living systems. Consequently, values are frequently treated either as products of individual psychology or as features of social and cultural history, with little explanation of how these perspectives connect.

Agencyâ€“Processâ€“Scale (APS) approaches this problem from a different direction. Rather than asking first which values people hold, APS asks what kind of phenomenon a value is. This shifts attention from the specific content of valuesâ€”such as justice, loyalty, freedom, or equalityâ€”to the organisational conditions that make valuing possible. The question is therefore not initially which values are correct, nor why particular societies endorse particular values, but what it means for anything to become valuable within the organisation of living systems.

Within APS, this question begins with biological evaluation. Living systems continuously distinguish conditions that support or undermine their organised persistence. Through biological evaluation, aspects of the world acquire significance in relation to viability-oriented organisation. Human values emerge from this broader evaluative foundation, but they are not reducible to individual biological responses. Instead, they arise when significance becomes organised, communicated, and stabilised within collective life through shared evaluation.

This interpretation neither reduces values to biology nor separates them from it. Human values are understood as organisationally real patterns that depend upon biological agency while emerging through the distinctive forms of coordination that characterise human societies. They therefore occupy the conceptual bridge between the biological organisation of living systems and the social organisation of collective life.

The purpose of this article is to establish this conceptual foundation. It defines human values within the explanatory architecture of APS, clarifies how they arise from biological evaluation and significance, distinguishes them from related concepts such as preferences, norms, morality, and ethics, and prepares the transition to Shared Evaluation, where the social organisation of values is examined in detail.

## Human Values as a Biological Phenomenon

At first sight, human values appear to belong exclusively to the domains of culture, morality, or reflective thought. They are commonly associated with ethical commitments, political ideals, religious beliefs, or personal convictions, and are therefore often regarded as phenomena that emerge only after biological explanation has ended. From this perspective, biology may explain the evolution of the human organism, while values are left to psychology, sociology, anthropology, or philosophy.

APS rejects this separation. It argues that although human values possess distinctive social and cultural forms, the capacity to value has biological foundations. The question is therefore not whether human values are biological in the same sense as metabolism or reproduction. Rather, it is whether the activity of valuing can be understood as a natural development of the evaluative organisation already present in living systems.

Throughout APS, biological evaluation refers to the continual activity through which living systems distinguish conditions according to their consequences for organised persistence. Organisms do not merely undergo environmental change; they respond differentially because aspects of their surroundings acquire significance in relation to their continuing viability. Food, shelter, mates, predators, pathogens, and social partners matter biologically because they affect the maintenance and re-establishment of the conditions under which living organisation persists.

This evaluative activity should not be confused with conscious judgement or moral reasoning. Biological evaluation is neither deliberation nor reflection. It is the ongoing organisation of agency through which living systems distinguish what contributes to, or detracts from, their continued viability. As APS has argued elsewhere, significance is generated through this evaluative organisation. What matters to an organism is therefore not imposed from outside but emerges through its own viability-oriented activity.

Human values arise from this biological foundation but cannot be reduced to it. Human beings possess forms of communication, learning, memory, symbolic representation, and collective organisation that enable significance to become socially organised across individuals and generations. Consequently, values are no longer confined to the immediate biological circumstances of individual organisms. They become shared, transmitted, debated, modified, and institutionalised within communities.

This transition does not represent a break between biology and culture. Rather, it marks a change in the organisation of evaluation. Biological evaluation explains how significance arises within living systems. Human values emerge when significance becomes organised through collective processes that stabilise what communities come to regard as important, desirable, or worthy of protection. The distinctive features of human values therefore depend upon the social organisation of evaluation, not upon the abandonment of their biological foundations.

Recognising this continuity is essential to the explanatory architecture of APS. If human values were treated as wholly independent of biological organisation, no coherent account could explain why valuing exists at all or how it emerged during evolution. Conversely, if values were reduced to biological mechanisms alone, their uniquely social and historical organisation would disappear from view. APS instead interprets human values as occupying the transition between these domains. They remain grounded in the evaluative organisation characteristic of living systems while acquiring new forms of organisation through communication, shared evaluation, and collective life.

This biological foundation does not explain which values particular societies adopt, nor does it determine whether those values are morally justified. Those questions belong to later stages of the APS social architecture. The present point is more fundamental. Human values become scientifically intelligible because they develop from an already existing biological capacity to generate significance through evaluation. The remaining sections of this article examine how that significance becomes organised into the stable patterns that constitute human values.

## Human Values in APS

Agencyâ€“Processâ€“Scale (APS) defines human values as stable patterns of significance organised through shared evaluation that guide the coordination of collective life.

This definition differs from many conventional accounts. Human values are not understood primarily as individual preferences, subjective attitudes, emotional dispositions, or abstract moral principles. Nor are they simply products of culture or historical convention. Instead, APS interprets values as organisationally real patterns that emerge when biological significance becomes stabilised through the collective organisation of evaluation.

<div class="aps-box">

### Human Values Are Not Preferences

Human values should not be confused with personal preferences.

Preferences may be temporary, individual, and context-dependent. Human values are relatively stable patterns of significance organised through shared evaluation that contribute to the coordination of collective life.

Preferences may express values, but they do not constitute them.

</div>

This account builds directly upon the preceding concepts of Biological Evaluation and Significance. Biological evaluation explains how living systems generate significance by distinguishing conditions according to their consequences for organised persistence. Significance therefore identifies what matters to an organism in relation to its continued viability. Human values arise when these patterns of significance become organised beyond the individual through communication, learning, memory, and shared forms of collective life.

Values should therefore be understood neither as isolated psychological states nor as external cultural abstractions. They exist within the organisation of relationships through which communities coordinate activity, establish expectations, resolve conflict, and maintain continuity across generations. Although individuals hold values, values themselves acquire stability only because they are continually reproduced through shared evaluation.

Within APS, values perform an organisational function. They provide relatively stable orientations that enable groups to coordinate behaviour under changing circumstances. In doing so, they reduce the complexity of collective decision-making by identifying what a community treats as important, desirable, worthy of protection, or requiring avoidance. Values therefore contribute to the organisation of collective agency rather than merely expressing individual opinion.

Because values organise significance rather than replace it, they remain open to revision. Human societies continually negotiate, reinforce, contest, and reorganise their values as circumstances change. This capacity for revision does not undermine the reality of values. On the contrary, it reflects their role within living systems that must continually maintain organised persistence under changing environmental and social conditions. Stability and adaptability therefore coexist within the organisation of values.

APS also distinguishes values from several closely related concepts. Values are not equivalent to preferences, which may be transient and individual. They are not identical with norms, which specify expected patterns of behaviour within a community. Nor are they the same as morality or ethics. Morality concerns the organisation of collective judgement concerning how persons ought to be treated, while ethics provides the reflective investigation of moral organisation. Values precede these developments by organising what communities collectively regard as significant before that significance becomes formalised into norms, moral systems, or ethical theories.

Human values therefore occupy a pivotal position within the explanatory architecture of APS. They form the organisational bridge between biological significance and the social institutions through which significance becomes collectively coordinated. Understanding values in this way allows APS to explain both their biological foundations and their distinctive social organisation without reducing one to the other.

The next step is to examine how values become shared. If values are stable patterns of significance organised within collective life, then an explanation is required of the processes through which individual evaluation becomes collectively organised. APS addresses this transition through the concept of Shared Evaluation, which explains how values become coordinated, communicated, stabilised, negotiated, and transformed within social organisation.

## Human Values and Collective Life

Human values do not exist simply as private beliefs or internal psychological states. Their biological significance is realised through collective life, where they contribute to the coordination of relationships among individuals and groups. APS therefore interprets values not only as patterns of significance but also as organisational principles that enable societies to maintain coherent forms of collective activity.

Every human community must continually coordinate cooperation, resolve conflict, allocate resources, transmit knowledge, organise responsibilities, and respond to changing environmental and social conditions. These activities cannot be sustained through individual biological evaluation alone. They require relatively stable patterns of shared significance that allow members of a community to anticipate one another's behaviour, recognise common priorities, and coordinate action across time. Human values provide part of this organisational stability.

Within APS, values contribute to collective organisation because they establish enduring orientations concerning what a community regards as important. They influence decisions without mechanically determining them. Individuals may disagree about the application of particular values, and societies may contest their relative importance, yet values nevertheless provide common reference points around which social coordination can occur. In this sense, values reduce uncertainty by stabilising expectations about what matters within collective life.

Communication plays a central role in this process. Values become socially effective only insofar as they can be expressed, interpreted, transmitted, and reproduced across individuals and generations. Language, symbolic practices, education, ritual, law, and other forms of communication all contribute to maintaining the continuity of shared significance. Through these processes, values become progressively detached from immediate biological circumstances and embedded within the enduring organisation of communities.

This organisation should not be understood as static. Human societies continually reinterpret their values in response to changing circumstances, new knowledge, technological innovation, demographic change, and interactions with other communities. The persistence of values therefore depends not upon immobility but upon their capacity to maintain organisational continuity through adaptive reorganisation. Stability and change are complementary features of living social systems rather than opposing alternatives.

APS consequently interprets values as enabling the coordination of collective agency across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Individuals participate in families, communities, institutions, nations, and wider global relationships, each of which depends upon partially overlapping systems of shared significance. Values therefore contribute to the integration of collective life by organising patterns of coordination that extend well beyond immediate interpersonal interactions.

Importantly, this account does not imply that every value contributes equally to organised persistence or that all socially established values are equally beneficial. Communities may sustain values that become maladaptive, internally contradictory, or sources of conflict under changing conditions. APS therefore distinguishes the organisational existence of values from any judgement concerning their truth, desirability, or moral legitimacy. Explaining how values organise collective life is distinct from evaluating whether particular values ought to be retained.

Understanding values as organisational principles clarifies their place within the broader APS architecture. Biological evaluation generates significance. Human values organise significance within collective life. The next question concerns the processes through which such organisation is achieved. APS addresses this through the concept of Shared Evaluation, which explains how individual patterns of significance become coordinated, communicated, negotiated, and stabilised across communities, thereby providing the immediate foundation for the emergence of social norms.

## Human Values, Social Norms, Morality, and Ethics

Human values occupy a distinct position within the explanatory architecture of APS. Although closely related to social norms, morality, and ethics, these concepts perform different explanatory roles. Maintaining these distinctions is essential if each is to contribute clearly to the organisation of biological and social explanation.

Human values organise what a community collectively regards as significant. They provide relatively stable orientations concerning what is considered important, desirable, or worthy of protection. Values therefore concern the organisation of significance rather than the regulation of behaviour itself.

Social norms arise from this organisation of values. Whereas values identify what matters, norms establish expectations concerning how members of a community are expected to behave in relation to those shared values. Norms therefore stabilise collective coordination by providing socially recognised patterns of conduct. They may be expressed formally through laws and institutions or informally through customs, traditions, and everyday practices, but in every case they organise behavioural expectations rather than significance itself.

Morality represents a further stage in this organisational development. Human communities do not merely coordinate behaviour; they also evaluate whether actions, institutions, and relationships ought to be regarded as acceptable or unacceptable in light of the values they collectively organise. Within APS, morality is therefore understood as the organisation of collective moral evaluation. It concerns how communities judge obligations, responsibilities, rights, harms, and legitimate forms of conduct. Morality does not create values but develops from the evaluative organisation already established through values and norms.

<div class="aps-box">

### Values Are Not Morality

Human values organise what communities collectively regard as significant.

Morality organises collective judgements concerning obligations, responsibilities, rights, harms, and legitimate conduct.

Values therefore provide part of the evaluative foundation from which morality develops, but they are not themselves a moral system. Not everything regarded as valuable has moral status, and explaining the existence of a value does not establish its moral legitimacy.

</div>

Ethics occupies a different explanatory role again. Ethics is not itself a system of values or moral rules but the reflective investigation of moral organisation. Ethical inquiry examines how moral systems arise, how they function, how they differ across communities, and how competing moral claims may be understood and evaluated. Ethics therefore belongs to the organisation of explanation rather than to the direct organisation of collective life.

Distinguishing these concepts prevents several common confusions. Values should not be equated with moral principles, because communities may regard many things as valuable without assigning them moral status. Likewise, norms are not identical with values, since similar values may be expressed through different normative practices in different societies. Nor should morality be reduced to ethics, because moral organisation exists independently of philosophical reflection upon it.

These distinctions also clarify the architecture of the APS social branch. Biological evaluation generates significance. Human values organise significance within collective life. Shared evaluation explains how values become collectively stabilised and negotiated. Social norms organise behavioural expectations. Morality organises collective moral judgement. Ethics investigates that moral organisation. Each concept therefore performs a distinct explanatory function while remaining integrated within a single organisational framework.

This progressive organisation allows APS to explain increasing forms of social complexity without abandoning the biological foundations established earlier in the framework. Human values thus occupy the pivotal transition between biological significance and the wider organisation of collective life, providing the conceptual foundation upon which norms, morality, and ethics are subsequently constructed.

## Human Values within the APS Architecture

Agencyâ€“Processâ€“Scale (APS) is organised as a progressively integrated explanatory framework in which each concept performs a distinct organisational role while preparing the conditions for those that follow. Human Values occupy a pivotal position within this architecture because they explain how biologically generated significance becomes organised within collective life. They therefore provide the conceptual bridge between the biological and social domains of the framework.

The preceding articles establish this progression. Life is understood as viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation. Biological agency enacts and sustains that organisation through ongoing activity. Biological evaluation continuously distinguishes conditions according to their consequences for organised persistence, thereby generating significance. Human Values extend this architecture by explaining how significance becomes stabilised within communities as relatively enduring patterns that guide collective coordination.

This position is neither arbitrary nor merely classificatory. Each transition within APS introduces a new organisational problem requiring explanation. Biological evaluation explains how individual organisms generate significance, but it does not by itself explain how multiple individuals come to coordinate that significance across families, communities, or societies. Human Values address this explanatory gap by identifying the stable patterns of shared significance that make collective organisation possible.

Human Values are therefore not the endpoint of the social branch but its point of departure. Once values exist as collectively organised patterns of significance, further organisational developments become possible. Shared Evaluation explains how those values are communicated, negotiated, reinforced, and modified through interaction. Social Norms stabilise expectations concerning behaviour. Social Organisation coordinates the activities of multiple agencies through institutions and enduring social structures. Moral Evaluation examines how collective actions affect others who possess moral standing. Morality organises those evaluations into relatively stable systems of judgement, while Ethics investigates their organisation through reflective inquiry.

Seen in this way, the social architecture of APS is not a sequence of isolated concepts but an increasingly differentiated organisation of collective evaluation. Each concept presupposes those preceding it while introducing new explanatory questions of its own. Human Values are indispensable within this progression because they explain the emergence of stable collective significance without conflating biological evaluation with social institutions or moral reasoning.

This architectural position also clarifies the relationship between continuity and novelty. Human Values remain continuous with the biological organisation of living systems because they ultimately derive from significance generated through biological evaluation. At the same time, they introduce genuinely new forms of organisation through communication, symbolic representation, cultural transmission, and collective coordination. APS therefore explains the emergence of social organisation without invoking a discontinuity between biology and culture or reducing one to the other.

Understanding Human Values within the broader APS architecture also clarifies the role of subsequent articles in the Social Organisation cluster. The present article establishes what human values are. Shared Evaluation explains how values become collectively organised. Social Norms explain how those organised values stabilise behavioural expectations. The remaining articles progressively investigate the increasingly complex forms of organisation that emerge from this foundation. The architecture therefore functions as an integrated explanatory framework rather than as a collection of independent concepts.

By locating Human Values within this progression, APS provides a coherent account of their explanatory role. Values are neither isolated psychological preferences nor abstract moral ideals. They are organisationally real patterns through which biological significance becomes coordinated within collective life, making possible the subsequent development of norms, institutions, morality, and ethics. Their position within the architecture reflects the distinctive explanatory work they perform in connecting the organisation of living systems with the organisation of human societies.

## Conclusion

Human values have traditionally been examined from the perspectives of psychology, anthropology, sociology, philosophy, and political theory. Each discipline has illuminated important aspects of valuing, yet no single account has satisfactorily explained how values relate to the organisation of living systems while also recognising their distinctive role within collective life. APS addresses this gap by situating human values within a unified explanatory architecture that connects biological organisation with social organisation.

This article has argued that human values are neither arbitrary cultural inventions nor timeless moral truths. Nor are they reducible to individual preferences, emotional dispositions, or biological mechanisms alone. Instead, APS interprets human values as stable patterns of significance organised through shared evaluation that guide the coordination of collective life. This definition preserves both their biological foundations and their distinctive social organisation without collapsing one into the other.

The argument has developed progressively through the conceptual architecture of APS. Biological evaluation explains how living systems generate significance through viability-oriented organisation. Human values emerge when that significance becomes organised collectively into relatively enduring orientations that coordinate social life. Values therefore represent a new level of organisational complexity while remaining continuous with the evaluative organisation characteristic of living systems.

This interpretation also clarifies the relationship between human values and adjacent concepts within the APS framework. Values organise collective significance. They do not themselves explain how significance becomes socially stabilised, how behavioural expectations are established, or how moral judgements are formed. Those questions belong respectively to Shared Evaluation, Social Norms, Morality, and Ethics. By distinguishing these explanatory roles, APS provides a coherent architecture in which each concept performs a specific organisational function while contributing to an integrated understanding of collective life.

Human values therefore occupy a pivotal position within APS. They provide the conceptual bridge between biological significance and the wider organisation of human societies. Without values, there is no coherent account of how biological evaluation becomes socially organised. Without this transition, the emergence of social norms, institutions, morality, and ethical reflection cannot be explained within a unified framework.

The next stage of this architecture concerns the organisation of values themselves. Human communities do not simply possess values; they continually communicate, negotiate, reinforce, contest, and transform them through collective activity. APS explains this transition through the concept of Shared Evaluation, which investigates how individual patterns of significance become organised into the enduring structures that sustain collective life.

Human values thus represent not the culmination of the APS social architecture but its point of departure. They establish the organisational foundation from which increasingly complex forms of social coordination emerge, providing the essential link between the organisation of living systems and the organisation of human societies.

The next article, *Shared Evaluation*, explains how individually generated significance becomes collectively organised into the enduring patterns that sustain human values and prepare the emergence of social norms.

# Information in Biology â€” An APS Clarification

> **Where this article fits:** This article clarifies the place of information within APS. It does not argue that informational descriptions are scientifically unimportant, nor does it attempt to replace information-theoretic explanations with a single alternative vocabulary. Its narrower claim is that biological information becomes explanatorily significant within already organised living systems whose activities are oriented toward viability and continued functioning. Information is therefore treated as relationally and organisationally situated rather than as the foundational property from which life, meaning, agency, or cognition can simply be derived.

Information has become one of the most pervasive explanatory concepts in modern biology. Genes are routinely described as carrying information, signalling pathways as transmitting it, nervous systems as processing it, and organisms as acquiring information about their environments. Similar language extends into developmental biology, systems biology, neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science. The success of these usages reflects genuine biological phenomena: living systems are sensitive to differences, coordinate activity through signalling, preserve and transform molecular patterns, and alter their behaviour in response to changing conditions.

The difficulty is that the word *information* does not have a single biological meaning. It may refer to statistical structure, transmitted signal, causal specificity, encoded sequence, functional dependence, semantic content, or a difference that matters to an organism. These uses can overlap, but they are not interchangeable. Confusion arises when the explanatory achievements of one informational concept are transferred without argument to another, or when the existence of informational relations is taken to show that information itself provides the foundational explanation of living organisation.

APS approaches this issue from the organisation of life rather than from an information-first starting point. Life is defined as viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation. Within such organisation, differences can acquire biological significance because they alter conditions relevant to continued functioning, regulation, development, behaviour, or persistence. Information, on this account, is not dismissed or reduced to something unreal. It is situated within the organisation that makes biological differences consequential.

This distinction matters because the question is not simply whether living systems use, transmit, or process information. They plainly do. The explanatory question is what makes some differences biologically significant, how that significance is organised, and what role informational description contributes to a specified biological explanandum. APS therefore treats information as an important but non-foundational concept whose biological significance must be understood in relation to agency, evaluation, semiosis, temporality, and organised persistence.

[[box:aps-box-meaning-develops-from-evaluative-significance]]

[[box:aps-box-semiosis-is-operational]]

# Why Information Became Central

The prominence of information in biology has strong historical and scientific justification. Twentieth-century developments in communication theory, cybernetics, molecular genetics, computation, and neuroscience provided powerful formal tools for analysing signalling, coding, transmission, uncertainty, regulation, and coordination. Shannon's mathematical theory of communication gave information a precise statistical meaning, while the growth of molecular biology encouraged informational descriptions of genetic sequence and gene expression. Cybernetic and computational approaches further reinforced the idea that biological systems could be understood in terms of signals, feedback, coding, and control.

These developments transformed biological inquiry. Informational concepts helped researchers describe the transmission of molecular patterns, the coordination of gene expression, sensory processing, neural signalling, developmental regulation, and communication among cells and organisms. Nothing in APS requires these explanatory achievements to be denied. An account of biological organisation that could not accommodate signalling, coding, communication, or information processing would be seriously incomplete.

The conceptual problem begins only when informational description is asked to do more than the relevant evidence establishes. Describing a signal as informative does not by itself explain why that signal matters to a living system. Identifying a genetic sequence does not by itself specify how its effects depend on cellular organisation, developmental context, or organismâ€“environment relations. Quantifying uncertainty reduction does not by itself establish biological meaning. Nor does demonstrating information processing show that information processing constitutes the organisation of life.

APS therefore distinguishes the scientific usefulness of informational approaches from claims about their explanatory scope. Its comparative methodology asks what an informational account explains for a specified target, what other organisational dependencies are required for that explanation, and whether an alternative account adds anything beyond redescription or conceptual reframing. The relevant comparison must be made against a matched explanandum rather than inferred from vocabulary alone.

This is also why APS does not treat information theory, cybernetics, computation, autonomy theory, or the Free Energy Principle as interchangeable competitors. They may address different questions, operate with different formal resources, and illuminate different aspects of biological organisation. Comparison becomes meaningful only when their explanatory targets overlap sufficiently for the contrast to be assessed.

# Shannon Information and Biological Meaning

A central distinction concerns Shannon information. In mathematical communication theory, information concerns statistical relations among possible signals and, in particular, the reduction of uncertainty associated with message transmission. This framework is exceptionally powerful because it permits communication to be analysed without requiring an account of what a message means to a sender or receiver.

That very strength also marks an important boundary. Shannon information does not, by itself, explain biological significance. A signal may be statistically informative while making no difference to the viability, regulation, or activity of a particular living system. Conversely, a difference of modest statistical complexity may have profound biological consequences if it alters a process upon which continued functioning depends.

The distinction is therefore not between "real" information and some merely metaphorical biological substitute. It is between different explanatory questions. Shannon theory characterises statistical structure and transmission. Biological explanation may additionally require an account of why a difference is consequential for a particular organised system.

Consider a chemical gradient encountered by a bacterium. The gradient can be described quantitatively in information-theoretic terms, but its biological significance depends on how sensitivity to that gradient participates in the bacterium's metabolism, regulation, movement, and prospects for continued functioning. The relevant biological relation is therefore not exhausted by the statistical properties of the signal. What matters is how the difference enters the organisation of activity.

APS uses the term **biological significance** for this viability-relative consequentiality. Biological significance does not require conscious interpretation, reflective judgement, or symbolic representation. It arises wherever differences alter conditions relevant to the organised persistence of a living system. In this sense, APS separates the statistical character of information from the biological question of what makes a difference matter.

[[box:aps-box-viability-grounds-evaluation]]

# Evaluation and Biological Information

APS connects biological significance with evaluation. Biological evaluation is the process through which agency generates significance. This does not imply deliberation, cognition, or conscious assessment. It refers to the organisation of activity in relation to differences that affect viability.

Living systems continuously encounter conditions that differ in their consequences. Some support continued functioning; others impair it. Some permit existing organisation to be maintained; others require regulatory adjustment, behavioural change, repair, or developmental reorganisation. These asymmetries are not imposed by an external observer. They arise because a living system must maintain and re-establish conditions required for its own persistence.

A nutrient gradient, for example, becomes biologically significant when sensitivity to it alters activity relevant to metabolic viability. A stress signal matters when it participates in regulatory changes affecting continued functioning. A developmental cue matters because its effects are organised within processes through which the developing system maintains continuity while changing its form. In each case, informational description can be useful, but the biological significance of the difference depends on the organisation within which it operates.

For this reason, APS does not say that evaluation chronologically occurs before all information, nor does it require the claim that information is causally inert until an evaluative mechanism acts upon it. The point is explanatory. Where *biological information* means information that matters to a living system, the account of that significance depends on the viability-relative organisation of the system concerned.

Information is therefore organisationally dependent in a specific sense: its biological significance is intelligible only in relation to the activities, constraints, and conditions through which living organisation persists. That claim should not be confused with a general assertion that informational explanations are explanatorily inferior. Whether an organisational account provides additional explanatory gain must be determined for a specified target and comparator.

# Semiosis and Informational Meaning

APS also distinguishes information from semiosis. Semiosis concerns the organisation through which differences function as signs within biological activity. It therefore directs attention not simply to the presence or transmission of a difference, but to the relation between that difference and the activity it modulates.

This distinction helps clarify why biological meaning need not begin with symbols or internal representations. A living system can be sensitive to a difference, respond selectively to it, and reorganise activity because of its viability-relevant consequences without representing that difference propositionally or consciously. The relevant meaning lies in the organised relation between difference, response, and continued functioning.

Semiosis therefore provides one route through which biological significance can be analysed without treating organisms as miniature human interpreters. A molecular concentration, environmental cue, or signalling event can function meaningfully because of the way it participates in the system's organisation. Its significance is relational: it depends on what the difference does within the ongoing activity of the living system.

On this account, information, semiosis, and meaning should not be collapsed into one another. Statistical information can exist without biological meaning. Biological significance can arise without symbolic representation. Semiosis concerns the organised use of differences within biological activity, while representation, where it occurs, introduces additional capacities that require separate explanation.

APS therefore resists an information-first progression in which signal structure alone is expected to generate biological meaning. The explanatory order is instead one of dependency: to explain why a difference counts as biologically informative, one may need to specify the living organisation for which it has consequences, the viability conditions relative to which those consequences matter, and the processes through which activity is modulated accordingly.

# Information Is Organisationally Derivative

To describe information as **organisationally derivative** is not to deny that informational relations are physically real or biologically important. The claim concerns explanatory dependence. Information becomes biological information because differences participate in an organised system for which alternative conditions have different consequences.

A nucleotide sequence, chemical signal, sensory event, or environmental cue does not acquire the same biological significance in every context. Its consequences depend on the organisation in which it occurs. Cellular machinery, metabolic state, developmental history, regulatory architecture, environmental conditions, and temporal context can all alter what a given difference does. The informational role of a sequence or signal is therefore relational rather than self-sufficient.

This is especially important when informational language is used foundationally. To say that an organism persists because information flows through it risks leaving unexplained the organisation that gives those informational relations their biological role. Living systems maintain boundaries, regulate internal conditions, repair damage, coordinate activity, and respond selectively to changing circumstances. Informational relations participate in these activities, but the activities cannot simply be read off from the abstract existence of information.

APS consequently places biological information within viability-oriented organisation rather than treating information as the substance from which such organisation is constructed. This is a claim about conceptual and explanatory placement, not a universal verdict on competing explanatory frameworks. An information-theoretic model may provide powerful causal or predictive understanding of a particular biological process. The APS question is whether that account also explains the viability-relative organisation relevant to the explanandum, and whether such an explanation is required in that case.

The distinction matters because biological explanation should not move automatically from the statement that information is present to the stronger claim that information explains the organisation within which it is biologically effective.

# Persistence, Evaluation, Semiosis, and Information

The relation among viability, evaluation, semiosis, meaning, information, and representation is better understood in APS as a set of explanatory dependencies than as a temporal ladder or hierarchy.

Viability provides the asymmetry through which some conditions support continued functioning while others threaten or disrupt it. Biological agency is the viability-oriented organisational activity through which those conditions are actively negotiated. Biological evaluation is the process through which such agency generates significance. Semiosis concerns the organisation of differences within that activity, allowing particular differences to function in ways that modulate the system's behaviour or regulation. Informational description becomes biologically significant when those meaningful differences participate in organised coordination.

Representation requires a further distinction. Not every biologically meaningful difference is represented. Representational capacities become relevant only where there is reason to attribute forms of organisation capable of standing in for conditions that are absent, future, hypothetical, or counterfactual. APS therefore does not define information by representation, nor representation by information alone.

These relations should not be interpreted as claims that every biological system instantiates a single fixed sequence or that each term names a separate ontological level. They identify different explanatory questions. Viability concerns the conditions of continued functioning; evaluation concerns viability-relative modulation; semiosis concerns how differences function within organised activity; information concerns structured differences and their roles in coordination; and representation concerns a more demanding form of mediated organisation.

This architecture helps explain why APS resists treating information as the single foundation from which the remaining biological phenomena are derived. The terms identify related but non-identical aspects of living organisation, and their explanatory relations must be established in relation to the biological target at issue.

# Genetic Information

Genetic information provides the most familiar biological example. Genes are often described as blueprints, programs, instructions, or repositories of biological information. Such language can be useful when it identifies sequence-dependent regularities or the transmission of heritable molecular patterns, but it can become misleading when it implies that genes operate independently of the living organisation in which they function.

Genetic sequences participate in development, cellular regulation, physiology, and evolutionary continuity. Their effects, however, depend on transcriptional and translational machinery, cellular conditions, regulatory networks, developmental context, metabolic activity, and interactions between organism and environment. A DNA sequence does not determine its biological consequences in isolation from these conditions.

This does not require replacing genetic explanation with a vague appeal to the "whole organism." It requires specifying the dependencies through which genetic differences become biologically effective. Genes may be causally indispensable in a particular explanation while still functioning within wider organised processes that determine when, where, and how their effects are realised.

APS therefore treats genetic information relationally. The informational role of a sequence depends on its participation in living organisation rather than on the sequence possessing a complete biological instruction independently of that organisation. This is compatible with recognising the enormous explanatory power of molecular genetics while resisting the stronger claim that genetic information alone supplies a sufficient account of development, agency, or life.

The point parallels broader critiques of information metaphors in biology: the usefulness of the metaphor depends on what explanatory work it is being asked to perform. Where sequence structure, transmission, or coding is the relevant target, informational language may be exact and productive. Where the explanandum concerns the organised persistence of a living system, further biological dependencies may need to be specified.

# Cognition and Information

Information processing also plays a central role in cognitive science. Many cognitive systems detect signals, integrate inputs, transform information, preserve state across time, and use previous conditions to modulate subsequent activity. APS has no reason to deny these phenomena. The question is whether cognition can therefore be identified with information processing as such.

APS treats cognition as the organisation of biological significance across time. On this account, cognition arises from living organisation but is not coextensive with life. Biological agency becomes cognitive when integrated biological significance modulates activity across a temporal field of viability-relevant possibilities in ways not exhausted by immediate or fixed regulation.

Information processing can participate in such organisation, but information processing alone does not establish cognition. Artificial systems can transform inputs, reduce uncertainty, classify patterns, optimise outputs, and manipulate representations without thereby satisfying the biological conditions APS associates with living agency or cognition. Conversely, some relatively simple living systems can exhibit context-sensitive, temporally integrated activity without requiring the assumption that they implement rich symbolic computation.

The important explanatory task is therefore not to oppose cognition and information processing. It is to determine what kind of organisation makes a particular informational process cognitive. APS directs attention to the integration of significance across time, the modulation of activity relative to viable possibilities, and the degree to which behaviour depends on more than immediate or fixed regulation.

This also prevents the language of information from doing hidden explanatory work. Saying that an organism "processes information" may accurately describe part of what occurs, but it does not by itself explain why particular inputs matter, how their significance is integrated with prior conditions, or how present activity is organised relative to possible future outcomes.

# Information and Representation

A similar distinction applies to representation. APS does not deny that representational capacities exist. It rejects only the assumption that biological meaning must begin with representation or that every informative biological relation therefore involves an internal representation.

Representation is a stronger explanatory commitment than sensitivity to or modulation by a difference. Some systems may respond directly to present conditions through organised regulatory dynamics. Others may preserve information across time, integrate prior states, model absent conditions, anticipate future possibilities, or organise activity around counterfactual alternatives. The latter cases provide stronger grounds for representational analysis.

The distinction is important because the terms *information*, *meaning*, and *representation* are often used as though they were interchangeable. APS separates them. A difference can have biological significance without being represented. Informational relations can contribute to regulation without constituting a model of the world. Representation becomes relevant when the organisation of activity involves a sufficiently rich relation to conditions that are not simply present in the immediate stimulus situation.

Information therefore does not need representation in order to matter biologically, while representation presupposes a prior organisation in which differences can already acquire significance. This is not a claim that representational systems appear at a sharply defined biological boundary. It is a methodological requirement to avoid inferring representation merely from the existence of signal processing or adaptive response.

# Information Across Biological Scales

Information is also encountered across very different spatial and temporal extents. At molecular scales, researchers analyse signalling pathways, gene regulation, metabolic coordination, and sequence relations. At organismal scales, informational language is used for perception, memory, learning, behavioural regulation, and anticipation. Across ecological contexts, organisms respond to environmental cues, communicate with other organisms, modify niches, and participate in distributed networks of biological interaction.

APS does not treat these as separate hierarchical levels governed by different kinds of causation. Scale identifies where persistence and explanatory dependencies are organised across spatial and temporal extents. Informational relations at one scale are materially implemented through processes occurring within and across others, and their explanatory relevance depends on the target being investigated.

A molecular signal, for example, may be locally characterised through receptor dynamics while also participating in organism-wide physiological regulation. A sensory cue may be processed through neural activity but acquire its biological significance from the behaviour and viability of the organism. An ecological signal may alter the activity of multiple organisms through materially specific interactions without requiring the ecosystem itself to be treated as an agent.

The general point is that biological information is context-sensitive. There is no single entity called *information* that performs the same explanatory role everywhere in biology. Informational concepts are most useful when the relevant relation, material implementation, biological target, and scale of organisation are made explicit.

# Information Without Life

The distinction between information and life becomes especially clear in artificial systems. Computers and communication networks process signals, encode and transform data, reduce uncertainty, classify patterns, optimise outputs, and generate complex responses. Contemporary artificial systems can display informational organisation of extraordinary sophistication.

These capacities demonstrate why information processing cannot by itself define life. A system may process information without being a viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation that actively maintains and re-establishes the conditions of its own persistence. Many artificial systems depend on externally supplied energy, maintenance, goals, infrastructure, repair, and operating conditions. Their informational complexity therefore does not by itself establish biological agency.

The same caution applies to cognition. Sophisticated inference, prediction, optimisation, or representation should not automatically be equated with biological cognition simply because both can be described informationally. APS distinguishes the formal capacities of a system from the organisation through which those capacities are generated and sustained.

This distinction is not intended to prejudge every possible artificial system. It identifies the explanatory criteria that would have to be examined. The question is not whether a system manipulates information, but what kind of organisation supports that manipulation, how the conditions of its persistence are maintained, and whether its activity is organised relative to viability in the relevant biological sense.

Information is therefore compatible with life but not sufficient for it. The existence of information processing establishes neither biological agency nor cognition without further organisational evidence.

# Information Within APS Explanatory Architecture

Within APS, information occupies an important but bounded explanatory role. APS begins from living organisation: life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation, and biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity. Process concerns how continuity is maintained despite change, while Scale concerns where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents. Agency, Process, and Scale are analytic projections of the same living organisation rather than separable components or hierarchical levels.

Information enters this architecture wherever differences participate in organised activity. Some differences alter viability conditions. Biological evaluation generates significance through the modulation of activity relative to those conditions. Semiosis concerns how differences function within this evaluative organisation. Informational relations can then describe the structured coordination, transmission, or transformation of differences that have become biologically consequential.

Cognition introduces further organisation across time. Where integrated biological significance modulates activity across a temporal field of viable possibilities, informational processes can become part of cognitive organisation. Representation may arise in still more specific circumstances, particularly where activity depends on absent, future, hypothetical, or counterfactual conditions.

This architecture does not imply that informational explanation should always be replaced by APS terminology. The appropriate explanatory vocabulary depends on the explanandum. If the question concerns channel capacity, sequence transmission, coding efficiency, or statistical uncertainty, information-theoretic analysis may be precisely what is required. If the question concerns why a difference matters to a living system, how significance arises, or how informational relations participate in organised persistence, an organisational account may also be necessary.

The APS contribution is therefore methodological as well as conceptual. It asks investigators to distinguish the explanatory target, identify the dependencies relevant to that target, specify their material implementation, and compare alternative accounts only where they genuinely address the same explanandum. Information is not excluded from biological explanation; it is placed within an architecture that makes its explanatory role explicit.

# Why Information Matters

Clarifying the place of information matters because informational vocabulary can obscure as much as it illuminates when several explanatory questions are compressed into one term. Distinguishing statistical information from biological significance helps prevent uncertainty reduction from being mistaken for meaning. Distinguishing information from semiosis clarifies how differences can function within living activity. Distinguishing information from representation prevents every biological response from being described as the manipulation of an internal model. Distinguishing information processing from cognition prevents a formal computational description from automatically settling a biological question.

These distinctions also help preserve the achievements of informational biology. There is no need to deny molecular coding, neural signalling, communication, or information processing in order to reject the stronger claim that information is the foundation of life. The more productive question is what explanatory role informational concepts perform in each context.

APS therefore naturalises biological information by locating it within materially implemented living organisation. Information becomes biologically significant because differences participate in processes that affect viable functioning, regulation, coordination, development, and behaviour. Its meaning is neither supplied by an external observer nor contained abstractly in the signal alone; it emerges from the relation between difference and organised biological activity.

This formulation also keeps the claim empirically assessable. If APS is to provide explanatory gain in a particular case, it must show what relevant dependency an informational account leaves unspecified, how that dependency is materially realised, and why including it improves explanation of the specified target. Conceptual preference for organisational language is not enough.

# Conclusion

Information is indispensable to contemporary biology, but its ubiquity should not be confused with explanatory priority. Living systems transmit signals, preserve molecular patterns, coordinate activity, respond selectively to environmental differences, and, in some cases, organise information across extended temporal horizons. Informational concepts are therefore legitimate and often powerful tools of biological explanation.

What APS rejects is the stronger inference that the existence of such relations makes information the foundational organisation of life. Biological information is always information *for or within an organised system*: a difference has biological significance because of how it participates in activities relevant to continued functioning. The explanatory task is consequently to understand the relation between informational structure and the viability-oriented organisation in which that structure becomes consequential.

Biological evaluation provides one part of this account by explaining how agency generates significance. Semiosis concerns the organisation of differences within activity. Cognition concerns the organisation of biological significance across time. Representation, where it occurs, adds further capacities for organising activity relative to absent or counterfactual conditions. These concepts are related, but none should be collapsed into information alone.

APS therefore treats information as real, scientifically important, and explanatorily useful while denying that it is sufficient by itself to define or explain life. Information is one of the ways organised living systems coordinate and sustain activity through time. Understanding its role requires attention not only to signals and statistical structure, but also to the living organisation within which differences come to matter.

## Key Point

Biological information is not rejected by APS and is not treated as merely metaphorical. Its biological significance depends on the organisation within which differences affect viability, regulation, coordination, and continued functioning. Information is therefore explanatorily important but organisationally situated rather than foundational.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

What explanatory role does information play in biology, and how should biological information be understood in relation to living organisation?

### Architectural Role

This Core article clarifies the status of information within APS. It distinguishes statistical information from biological significance and explains why informational relations become biologically consequential within viability-oriented living organisation. Its principal function is to establish the relationship among information, evaluation, semiosis, meaning, representation, cognition, and organised persistence without reducing these concepts to one another.

The following concepts establish explanatory dependencies presupposed by this article. These are dependencies within the APS architecture rather than chronological stages, hierarchical levels, or independent components of living systems.

In doing so, it connects the APS accounts of agency, evaluation, semiosis, meaning, cognition, and representation while providing a controlled basis for comparison with informational approaches in theoretical biology.

## Inheritance as Organisational Continuity

Within the Evolution domain, inheritance explains the continuity that makes evolutionary transformation possible. If natural selection accounts for the differential persistence of living systems, inheritance explains how viable organisation persists across generations in the first place. In APS, inheritance is therefore understood as the continuity of viability-oriented organisation through time rather than the transmission of privileged biological components.

Inheritance is not the transfer of a substance, code, or informational entity from one generation to the next. It is the reliable reconstitution of a living system capable of sustaining itself as a viability-oriented organisation. Evolution depends upon this continuity because transformation can accumulate only when living organisation is repeatedly re-established across generations. What persists through evolutionary history is therefore not a gene, structure, or molecule considered in isolation, but a pattern of organisation capable of maintaining viability within changing circumstances.

Inheritance stabilises continuity across generations and thereby provides the foundation upon which variation, adaptation, and selection can operate. Without inheritance there could be no cumulative evolutionary transformation because there would be no enduring organisational continuity to transform. Inheritance therefore occupies a central position within the APS continuity architecture. Biological agency sustains viability-oriented activity. Viability enables organised persistence. Inheritance reproduces that persistence across generations, providing the continuity upon which fitness, natural selection, and evolutionary transformation depend. Evolutionary change therefore presupposes inherited continuity before it can become historically differentiated.

## Beyond Component Transmission

[[box:inheritance-is-not-information-transfer]]

Traditional accounts of inheritance often focus on the transmission of genetic material. Genes undoubtedly participate in biological continuity, but APS rejects the view that inheritance can be reduced to the transfer of genes or any other privileged component. The central question is not which component is passed on, but how viable organisation is reliably re-established across generations.

Genes do not produce biological continuity independently. Their effects depend upon the organisational contexts in which they are expressed, the developmental processes through which they become biologically effective, and the environmental conditions that support the persistence of living systems. A gene contributes to inheritance only insofar as it participates in a broader network of organisational relations that collectively sustain viability. Biological continuity therefore emerges from the organisation within which genes participate rather than from genes considered in isolation.

This perspective shifts attention away from components and toward organisation itself. Biological continuity does not arise because particular elements are transmitted unchanged through time. Rather, continuity emerges because living systems repeatedly reconstruct patterns of organisation capable of maintaining themselves. Genes are therefore contributors to inheritance rather than its explanatory foundation. Their significance derives from the role they play within an ongoing process of organisational continuity.

APS thus reframes inheritance from a problem of component transmission to a problem of organisational persistence. The fundamental question becomes how living systems reliably regenerate viability-oriented organisation despite continual material turnover, developmental transformation, and environmental change.

## Development as Reconstitution

Inheritance becomes biologically effective through development. Development is the process by which inherited organisation is reconstituted as an operational living system. In APS, development is therefore not secondary to inheritance but one of the primary mechanisms through which inheritance is realised.

This understanding differs significantly from accounts that treat development as the execution of a genetic programme. Living systems do not simply unfold pre-specified instructions. Instead, development reconstructs a dynamic, constraint-closed organisation through the coordinated interaction of molecular, cellular, physiological, behavioural, and environmental processes. What emerges is not the implementation of a blueprint but the re-establishment of a viable system.

Development is the point at which continuity becomes active. Through developmental processes, inherited organisational relations are rebuilt and integrated into a functioning whole capable of maintaining itself. Continuity is therefore enacted rather than merely stored. The persistence of a lineage depends not only on what is inherited but also on the successful developmental reconstruction of inherited organisation.

Inheritance and development consequently form a single continuity architecture. Inheritance provides the conditions through which viable organisation can be re-established, while development performs that re-establishment through the coordinated reconstruction of living organisation. Neither process is intelligible in isolation because each depends upon the other for its biological significance. Together they explain how living systems preserve continuity despite continual material and organisational change.

This continuity architecture extends beyond inheritance and development alone. The successful developmental reconstitution of viable organisation contributes directly to the continuity of persistence-sustaining organisation across generations. In this sense, development helps establish the continuity upon which fitness and natural selection subsequently operate.

## The Role of Environment in Continuity

APS also rejects the view that inheritance occurs solely within organisms. Living systems inherit within ecological and developmental contexts that contribute directly to the maintenance of continuity across generations. Organismâ€“environment coupling is therefore not external to inheritance but part of the continuity architecture through which viability is sustained.

Every generation develops within environmental conditions that both constrain and support developmental reconstruction. These conditions may include ecological niches, parental modifications of the environment, symbiotic relationships, behavioural traditions, and other stabilising structures that contribute to the reliable re-establishment of viable organisation. Such relations are not passive backgrounds against which inheritance occurs. They actively participate in making continuity possible.

From this perspective, inheritance extends beyond internal biological components to encompass the organised relations through which developmental and ecological continuity are maintained. The persistence of a lineage depends not only on what occurs within organisms but also on the stability of the broader relational systems that support developmental reconstitution.

This broader conception of inheritance aligns naturally with APS's emphasis on organismâ€“environment coupling. Living systems persist through ongoing interactions with their environments, and these interactions frequently contribute to the continuity of viable organisation across generations. Inheritance therefore concerns the continuation of organisational relations rather than the transmission of isolated biological entities.

  <img
    src="/assets/diagrams/evolution-inheritance.png"
