## From Observation to Explanation

The contemporary literature on plant agency has fundamentally changed what requires explanation in plant biology. It has established that plants are not passive organisms governed by fixed developmental programmes or simple stimulusâ€“response mechanisms. Instead, they exhibit distributed regulation, long-distance coordination, physiological plasticity, environmental responsiveness, ecological interaction, and remarkable organisational continuity throughout their lives. These observations are no longer exceptional claims but increasingly form part of the empirical foundation upon which modern plant biology is being built.

The central question has therefore shifted. The challenge is no longer to demonstrate that plants exhibit organised, adaptive behaviour, but to understand why such diverse phenomena consistently appear together. Contemporary theories frequently answer this question by emphasising one aspect of living organisation above others. Some locate the foundations of agency in distributed cognition, others in autopoietic organisation, embodied interaction, biosemiotic interpretation, electrical signalling, or ecological construction. Each perspective illuminates genuine features of plant life, yet each also approaches the problem through its own conceptual language and explanatory priorities.

APS approaches the same body of evidence from a different direction. Rather than asking which organisational feature gives rise to agency, it asks what biological requirement makes all of these organisational features necessary. This seemingly modest shift changes the structure of the explanation. Instead of treating signalling, cognition, semiosis, or ecological interaction as alternative foundations of agency, APS understands them as complementary processes through which living systems maintain themselves under continually changing conditions.

The organising principle is viability-oriented organised persistence. Living systems do not merely exist; they must continually sustain the organisation that makes continued existence possible. Every moment of life requires the coordination of processes that preserve integrity despite material turnover, developmental change, environmental uncertainty, injury, competition, and reproduction. Agency is therefore not an optional characteristic acquired by sufficiently complex organisms but the continual activity through which viable organisation is maintained. Once this principle becomes the explanatory starting point, the diverse discoveries of contemporary plant biology no longer appear as separate phenomena requiring separate theories. They become different expressions of the same organisational necessity.

## Why Plants Are Agents

APS defines biological agency as viability-oriented, self-regulating activity through which living systems sustain, modulate, and continually recreate the conditions of their own organised persistence. This definition differs from many contemporary accounts not because it rejects signalling, cognition, or behaviour, but because it asks a more fundamental question. Before an organism can learn, anticipate, communicate, or make decisions, it must first remain alive. Every subsequent organisational capacity therefore depends upon the continual preservation of viability.

Plants illustrate this relationship with exceptional clarity. Unlike many animals, they cannot respond to changing conditions simply by moving elsewhere. Every challenge must instead be met through continual internal reorganisation. Growth patterns alter as light conditions change. Root systems expand, contract, or redirect themselves as soils become more or less favourable. Water transport is continually adjusted to changing environmental demands. Developmental pathways remain responsive throughout the life of the organism, while defensive systems, reproductive strategies, and symbiotic relationships are all reorganised according to changing circumstances. These activities differ profoundly in mechanism and timescale, yet they remain united by a common biological objective: sustaining the organisation that allows the plant to continue living.

From this perspective, agency is fundamentally regulatory before it becomes behavioural. Behaviour is one expression of agency, not its definition. The continual coordination of development, physiology, metabolism, ecological interaction, and environmental responsiveness all belong to the same organisational process because each contributes to maintaining viable organisation. APS therefore understands agency as the activity that integrates these diverse processes into the continuing persistence of the living organism.

## Signalling Serves Agency

Among the most important achievements of contemporary plant biology has been the demonstration that plants possess sophisticated systems of internal communication. Electrical activity coordinates responses across tissues. Hydraulic signals redistribute physiological activity throughout the organism. Hormonal networks integrate development with changing environmental conditions. Mechanical and chemical signals continually modify growth, defence, reproduction, and ecological interaction. Together these discoveries have transformed our understanding of how plants achieve coordinated organisation without nervous systems.

APS fully accepts the significance of these discoveries while proposing a different explanatory relationship between signalling and agency. Contemporary discussions sometimes present increasingly sophisticated signalling systems as the basis from which agency emerges. APS reverses this explanatory direction. Living systems require signalling because they are already agents engaged in maintaining their own viability. Communication systems evolve and diversify because coordinated regulation becomes progressively more effective as organisms increase in complexity. Signalling therefore serves agency rather than creating it.

This distinction provides a unified way of interpreting the extraordinary diversity of biological communication. Animals rely heavily upon nervous systems, plants upon distributed physiological networks, fungi upon filamentous organisation, and microbial communities upon entirely different modes of coordination. The mechanisms differ because evolutionary history has produced multiple solutions to the problem of biological organisation. The underlying requirement, however, remains constant. Every living system must coordinate activity in ways that preserve viability across changing internal and external conditions. APS therefore interprets signalling as one family of regulatory processes through which agency is enacted rather than as the origin of agency itself.

[[box:signalling-does-not-create-agency]]

## Plant Cognition Without Anthropomorphism

Few areas of contemporary biology have generated more discussion than the proposal that plants exhibit forms of cognition. Experimental evidence for learning, memory, anticipatory regulation, environmental discrimination, and flexible behavioural coordination has challenged the long-standing assumption that cognition requires neurons or brains. These discoveries have encouraged researchers to reconsider not only the nature of plants but also the biological meaning of intelligence itself.

APS welcomes this reconsideration while introducing an important conceptual clarification. Agency, cognition, intelligence, and consciousness describe different aspects of living organisation and should not be treated as interchangeable concepts. Every living organism must regulate itself if it is to remain viable, but not every organism necessarily exhibits the same forms or degrees of cognitive organisation. Conflating these concepts risks obscuring rather than clarifying the biological phenomena under investigation.

From an APS perspective, the capacities commonly described as learning, memory, anticipation, and decision-making can all be understood as organisational extensions of viability-oriented regulation. Learning modifies future regulatory responses in light of previous experience. Memory preserves aspects of organisational history that remain relevant to future viability. Anticipation prepares the organism for conditions that have not yet occurred but are biologically probable. Decision-making coordinates alternative courses of action when multiple regulatory demands compete. Each represents a distinct mode of biological organisation, yet each ultimately contributes to the same underlying task of sustaining organised persistence.

This interpretation allows APS to recognise the remarkable sophistication of plant organisation without either diminishing its significance or relying upon anthropomorphic language. Plant cognition becomes neither a metaphor borrowed from animal biology nor a claim requiring controversial assumptions about consciousness. Instead, it is understood as one important organisational expression of biological agency itself. In doing so, APS preserves the empirical achievements of contemporary plant cognition while locating them within a broader explanatory framework capable of encompassing all living systems.

[[box:agency-is-not-intelligence]]

## One Organisational Principle, Many Biological Expressions

The growing diversity of theories surrounding plant agency reflects an important development in contemporary biology. Researchers working in different disciplines have approached living organisation from different directions, each emphasising phenomena that had previously received insufficient attention. Autopoiesis has highlighted the self-producing organisation of living systems. Enactivism has explored the inseparability of organism and environment in biological activity. Biosemiotics has examined the emergence of biological meaning through living interactions. Plant electrophysiology has revealed unexpectedly sophisticated systems of distributed communication, while ecological approaches have demonstrated that organisms continually construct, modify, and inhabit the environments that sustain them.

Viewed independently, these perspectives can appear to compete for explanatory priority. Each proposes a different language through which biological organisation should be understood, and each naturally emphasises those aspects of living systems most visible within its own research tradition. Yet the remarkable convergence of their empirical observations suggests that the apparent diversity may conceal a deeper unity.

APS proposes that this unity lies in the organisation of viability itself. Every one of these theoretical perspectives describes processes through which living systems maintain, regulate, or extend the conditions necessary for their continued persistence. Autopoiesis explains how organisation continually reproduces itself. Enactivism explains how that organisation remains dynamically coupled to its surroundings. Biosemiotics explains how environmental differences acquire biological significance because they matter for viability. Signalling coordinates activity throughout the organism, while ecological interactions extend regulation beyond the immediate boundaries of the individual. Each therefore contributes an essential perspective on the same underlying organisational reality.

Rather than replacing these theories, APS provides an explanatory grammar through which their contributions become mutually intelligible. Their differences remain important because they illuminate different organisational processes, but they need no longer be understood as competing accounts of life. They become complementary descriptions of how viability-oriented organised persistence is achieved across different biological systems, different mechanisms, and different scales of organisation.

## Plant Agency Beyond the Individual

One of the most important developments in recent plant biology has been the growing recognition that agency cannot always be understood solely by examining individual organisms in isolation. Plants continually regulate their relationships with soils, microbial communities, fungal symbionts, neighbouring plants, and wider ecological systems. Root exudates modify the physical and biological properties of soils. Mycorrhizal partnerships alter nutrient acquisition, development, and resilience. Volatile organic compounds influence defensive responses both within individual plants and across neighbouring communities. In each case, biological organisation extends beyond the visible boundaries of the organism itself.

APS interprets these observations as natural consequences of viability-oriented organisation rather than as exceptions requiring separate explanatory principles. Organisms remain viable by regulating the relationships upon which their persistence depends. As those relationships become increasingly complex, regulation necessarily extends into the surrounding environment. Agency therefore cannot be confined to events occurring within the physical boundaries of the organism alone. It encompasses the continual organisation of organismâ€“world coupling through which viable persistence is achieved.

This perspective also clarifies why ecological organisation occupies such a central position within APS. Ecology is not simply the external context in which organisms exist. It forms part of the organisational processes through which living systems continually sustain themselves. Plant agency therefore reveals that biological organisation is simultaneously physiological, developmental, behavioural, and ecological. These are not separate explanatory domains but interconnected expressions of a single organisational reality unfolding across multiple scales.

## What APS Contributes

The principal contribution of APS is not to introduce another theory of plant agency but to provide a common explanatory framework capable of integrating the diverse insights emerging across contemporary biology. The remarkable expansion of research into signalling, cognition, ecology, development, electrophysiology, biosemiotics, and organismâ€“environment interaction has greatly enriched our understanding of plant life. At the same time, it has produced an increasingly diverse conceptual landscape in which different explanatory languages often coexist without an obvious organising principle.

APS addresses this problem by shifting attention from particular mechanisms to the biological organisation those mechanisms collectively sustain. Signalling is understood in relation to regulation. Regulation is understood in relation to agency. Agency is understood in relation to viability. Viability is understood in relation to organised persistence. In this way, phenomena that initially appear conceptually distinct become integrated within a single explanatory architecture.

This approach also provides a framework that extends naturally beyond plants themselves. The same organisational principles apply across animals, fungi, microbial communities, and other living systems despite the enormous diversity of mechanisms through which biological organisation is achieved. APS therefore does not propose a specifically botanical theory. It proposes that plant biology has revealed particularly clearly a more general principle governing life itself. By demonstrating that agency does not depend upon brains or nervous systems, plants expose the organisational foundations shared by all living systems.

[[box:why-plants-changed-biology]]

## Conclusion

The emergence of plant agency represents one of the most important conceptual developments in contemporary biology. It has challenged assumptions that long confined agency to organisms possessing nervous systems and has revealed plants as active participants in generating, regulating, and sustaining their own biological organisation. Research across plant physiology, ecology, development, cognition, electrophysiology, autopoiesis, enactivism, and biosemiotics has collectively transformed the questions that biology now asks about living systems.

APS fully embraces this transformation. Rather than questioning whether plants are genuine biological agents, it asks what makes agency biologically necessary in the first place. Its answer is that agency arises from the continual organisation of viability. Living systems persist only because they continually regulate the conditions that allow organised persistence to continue. Signalling, learning, memory, anticipation, ecological interaction, and environmental modification therefore become different organisational expressions of the same underlying biological imperative.

From this perspective, the growing diversity of contemporary theories no longer represents a collection of competing explanations but a progressively richer understanding of living organisation viewed from different directions. APS neither replaces these perspectives nor reduces their distinct contributions. Instead, it provides an explanatory framework within which they can be understood together, revealing the common organisational principles that unite them.

Plant agency therefore becomes more than a specialised topic within botany. It becomes one of the clearest demonstrations that life is fundamentally an organised, viability-oriented process whose defining characteristic is neither structure nor mechanism alone, but the continual activity through which living systems sustain, reorganise, and extend the conditions of their own persistence.

## Introduction

Plant cognition has occupied an unusual place in the development of the Agencyâ€“Processâ€“Scale framework. It was one of the problems through which APS was first publicly articulated, and it later became a case against which the framework's developing account of cognition and biological explanation could be tested.

The result is not a simple history in which an early position was replaced by a later one. Important commitments remained stable. Others became more sharply differentiated. Still others arose through research elsewhere within APS and were subsequently brought back to the plant-cognition problem. The standards governing explanatory claims also changed.

Plant cognition therefore provides a longitudinal case through which APS itself can be examined. The question is not simply whether the framework once attributed cognition to plants and now does so more cautiously. It is what that change reveals about the development of the concepts and standards of biological explanation through which the attribution is made.

## 1. Plant Cognition as an Originating APS Problem

The 2025 paper *Biological Agency as the Context for Plant Cognition* placed biological Agency at the centre of the problem (Spencer 2025). Its starting point was that cognition should not be approached by assuming that familiar human or neural manifestations determine what cognition must be throughout biology. Plants therefore mattered not because they could be assimilated to animals, but because they forced attention towards the biological organisation within which capacities conventionally described as cognitive arise.

Agency supplied that context. Living systems were treated as active rather than passive organisations: they regulate their relations with changing conditions, maintain their viability, and modify activity in ways relevant to continued functioning. The original treatment of biological cognition was correspondingly broad. Capacities associated with information processing, prioritisation, retention, learning, prediction, problem solving, and adaptive modulation could be considered within a biologically general account rather than being restricted in advance to organisms possessing nervous systems.

This formulation performed an important conceptual task. It relocated the plant-cognition question within biology. Whether plants were cognitive could not be settled merely by noting the absence of brains, nervous systems, consciousness, or human-like representation.

At the same time, the originating formulation placed considerable explanatory weight on Agency. The distinctions that later APS would draw among biological Agency, Biological Evaluation, Significance, Integration, and Cognition did not yet structure the problem in their developed form. Adaptive biological organisation and biological cognition consequently stood closer together than they would in later APS.

That difference should not be retrospectively removed. The 2025 position needs to be understood in the conceptual terms available to APS at that time rather than rewritten as though the developed architecture were already fully present.

## 2. What Remained Stable

Development did not remove the biological starting point of the original argument.

APS continues to reject the assumption that cognition can be defined simply by possession of a nervous system. It also continues to distinguish cognition from consciousness, reflective thought, linguistic reasoning, and human intelligence. The absence of those capacities cannot by itself decide whether a biological system is cognitive.

Agency also remains fundamental. Developed APS defines biological Agency as viability-oriented organisational activity. Cognition, if present, occurs within such activity rather than constituting an independent faculty added to an otherwise passive organism.

The continuing importance of the 2025 argument therefore lies partly in the question it established. Plants confront theories of cognition with organisms displaying complex sensing, signalling, regulation, developmental plasticity, historical responsiveness, and coordinated organismâ€“environment relations without animal neural architecture. Those phenomena remain biologically significant regardless of where the cognition boundary is eventually placed.

What changes is not their existence or importance. What changes is what APS considers sufficient to warrant the further attribution of Cognition.

This distinction matters. A more restrictive attribution of cognition need not imply that plants have become explanatorily less interesting, that the earlier observations were mistaken, or that neural criteria have been restored by another route. The continuity lies in treating plant activity as a serious problem of biological organisation. The development lies in differentiating more precisely what kind of organisation different plant phenomena establish.

## 3. When Agency Was No Longer Enough

An important development occurred as APS differentiated what Life is from what living systems do.

The published Agency thesis characterised biological Agency as the defining activity of Life (Spencer 2026). Developed APS retains that insight while making a sharper distinction. Life is defined as **viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation**. Biological Agency is **viability-oriented organisational activity**. Agency is therefore the activity through which living organisation is enacted and maintained, not the complete definition of that organisation.

This distinction also clarifies the relation between Agency and Cognition.

If Agency characterises living activity generally, Agency cannot by itself establish Cognition. An organism may sense relevant conditions, regulate internal variables, alter activity in relation to viability, repair damage, coordinate distributed processes, and respond flexibly to environmental change while the question of cognition remains open.

This is not a reduction in the importance of Agency. It is a differentiation of explanatory tasks.

Agency identifies what living systems do as active organisations. Cognition requires a further question about how biologically significant conditions are organised across time. The fact that an activity is adaptive, flexible, or viability-relevant may contribute evidence to that question, but it no longer answers it in advance.

For plant cognition, this changes the burden of attribution. Demonstrating sophisticated plant Agency establishes an important biological result. It does not automatically establish a cognitive one.

## 4. Evaluation, Significance and Integration

A further change became possible as APS differentiated the organisational pathway connecting Agency and Cognition.

The developed architecture can be represented in part as:

**Life â†’ Agency â†’ Biological Evaluation â†’ Significance â†’ Integration â†’ Cognition**

The sequence expresses dependency within one living organisation, not a hierarchy, chronology, or series of independent components.

**Biological Evaluation** identifies the process through which Agency generates Significance. Living activity is not indifferent to conditions. Some differences bear differently on viability, and the system's organisation can modulate activity accordingly.

**Significance** identifies what is generated through this viability-relative differentiation. It is relationally real: conditions matter in relation to the organisation and persistence of the living system without requiring conscious interpretation or reflective judgement.

This immediately creates a distinction that was less explicit in the originating treatment of plant cognition. A plant can evaluate conditions biologically. Those conditions can acquire significance for the plant. Neither fact alone establishes cognition.

**Integration** introduces another distinction. Significance may be organised into functional unity across interacting processes without that integration automatically becoming cognitive. Distributed signalling, physiological coordination, developmental regulation, and organism-wide modulation can therefore be substantial organisational achievements while remaining insufficient by themselves to settle the cognition question.

Cognition occupies a further position in this architecture. Its canonical APS definition is:

**Cognition is the organisation of biological significance across time.**

The importance of this architecture for plant cognition is discriminatory. It allows observations previously gathered under a broad heading of biological cognition to be separated according to the explanatory work they actually support.

It may demonstrate Evaluation and Significance without demonstrating Cognition. It may demonstrate extensive Integration while the cognitive status of that integration remains unresolved.

The conceptual architecture therefore does not diminish the phenomena. It increases the number of explanatory distinctions available for understanding them.

## 5. A Development That Was Not Linear

It would be tempting to turn these distinctions into a simple developmental sequence: APS began with a broad conception of plant cognition, differentiated Agency from Evaluation, Significance, Integration, and Cognition, and consequently withdrew its earlier attribution.

The historical record does not support that reconstruction.

During June 2026, the canonical Plant Cognition article still described plants positively as exhibiting a minimal, non-neural form of biological cognition grounded in viability-oriented evaluative organisation. A July version remained comparatively permissive, presenting plant cognition as a minimal form of evaluative organisation and plants as an important case for understanding cognition as a graded biological phenomenon.

Yet important parts of the more differentiated APS architecture were already present during this period. By July, the canonical architecture explicitly distinguished Life, Agency, Biological Evaluation, Significance, Integration, and Cognition.

The coexistence matters.

Conceptual differentiation did not automatically produce the later plant-cognition assessment. Nor did the appearance of intermediate terms make the consequences of those distinctions immediately determinate. APS could distinguish Evaluation from Cognition conceptually while still interpreting sufficiently elaborate evaluative organisation in plants as minimally cognitive.

This is why the development cannot be represented adequately as **early error â†’ conceptual correction â†’ mature answer**.

Several strands were developing at different rates. The Lifeâ€“Agency distinction clarified the status of Agency. The Evaluationâ€“Significanceâ€“Integration architecture provided new intermediate explanatory distinctions. Cognition research investigated what additional organisation should count as cognitive. Comparative methodology separately tightened the conditions under which explanatory gain could be claimed.

These developments eventually converged on the plant problem, but their convergence should not be projected backwards as a predetermined sequence.

The historical case therefore contains genuine continuity alongside genuine change. The originating biological question persisted even while the conceptual resources available for answering it were being reorganised.

## 6. A More Discriminating Boundary for Cognition

The dependency architecture made it possible to distinguish Cognition from earlier forms of viability-oriented organisation. It did not, by itself, determine where the boundary should be placed.

That required a more specific problem: what differentiates cognition from sophisticated biological regulation?

APS minimal-cognition research increasingly focused on this boundary. Immediate responsiveness is insufficient. Fixed regulatory control is insufficient. History-dependent modification or hysteresis is not automatically cognitive. Even retention of prior effects cannot decide the issue if present activity remains exhaustively explainable through fixed or immediate regulatory organisation.

The developing criterion therefore placed greater weight on how biological significance is organised across time and on whether activity is modulated relative to materially available, viability-relevant possibilities rather than merely following a fixed regulatory relation.

This introduces what APS describes as **counterfactual depth**. The expression does not imply conscious consideration of alternatives or representation of hypothetical futures. It asks whether the organisation of present activity depends on a structured field of possibilities that matters materially to the system, rather than being exhausted by immediate or fixed regulation.

The distinction is particularly important for plants because many candidate phenomena are temporally extended. Stress history can alter later responsiveness. Developmental states can retain consequences of earlier conditions. Priming can modify subsequent responses. Such phenomena establish biologically consequential organisation across time.

They do not automatically establish cognition.

The relevant question becomes whether temporal organisation provides evidence for the organisation of biological significance across viability-relevant possibilities in a way not exhausted by an adequate non-cognitive regulatory account.

Plant cognition was clearly relevant to this developing boundary problem. The historical record does not, however, establish that plant cognition aloneâ€”or even primarilyâ€”caused APS to formulate counterfactual depth or the later minimal-cognition criterion. Those developments belong to a broader APS cognition research programme and apply across biological cases.

Their importance here lies in what became possible when they were returned to plants: phenomena could now be investigated without either dismissing their complexity or classifying that complexity as cognitive by default.

## 7. From Interpretation to Comparative Explanation

A second development changed the plant-cognition problem in a different way.

Conceptual architecture asks how a phenomenon can be understood. Comparative explanatory methodology asks what explanatory claim is warranted relative to alternatives.

APS increasingly separated those questions.

A framework may organise observations coherently, connect phenomena that were previously treated separately, or supply a conceptually attractive interpretation. None of those achievements by itself demonstrates additional explanatory capacity.

Comparative explanatory methodology therefore begins with a specified explanandum. The relevant question is not whether APS can describe plants as cognitive, or whether another approach can describe the same phenomena as regulation. The question is what particular biological phenomenon requires explanation and what each candidate account explains about it.

The strongest adequate comparator must then be reconstructed on its own terms. For a proposed case of minimal cognition, this normally means asking whether an adequate non-cognitive account based on regulation, physiological memory, developmental plasticity, signalling, or another materially supported process already explains the target phenomenon.

Only then does a claim of **explanatory gain** become meaningful.

The operative question becomes:

**For this explanandum, relative to the strongest adequate comparator, what additional explanatory contribution is established?**

This methodological change has consequences for APS itself. The framework is not entitled to a positive result because a phenomenon can be redescribed successfully in APS terminology. Nor can the architecture of Agency, Evaluation, Significance, Integration, and Cognition guarantee that any particular biological system crosses the cognitive boundary.

A controlled comparison must admit different outcomes. A proposed cognitive explanation may demonstrate bounded explanatory gain. The accounts may prove complementary. No additional gain may be demonstrated. The evidence may remain unresolved. The accounts may turn out not to address sufficiently matched explanatory targets.

Null and adverse results are therefore legitimate outcomes of the method rather than failures to vindicate APS.

There is no basis in the closed historical record for claiming that plant cognition caused APS to develop this comparative methodology. The methodology emerged as a programme-level response to broader problems of comparing biological explanations and research programmes. Its importance to the present history lies in its subsequent application to a problem with which APS had been associated from its originating formulation.

That application changes the status of the question. Plant cognition becomes not only something APS interprets but something against which APS's own explanatory discipline can be tested.

## 8. Returning to Plants

When these conceptual and methodological developments are brought together, the plant-cognition problem takes a different form.

The current APS assessment does not ask for a global verdict on whether â€œplants are cognitive.â€ It asks whether specified plant phenomena warrant cognitive explanation relative to the strongest adequate non-cognitive account.

This permits an asymmetric result.

Plant Agency is robust. Plants regulate their relations with changing conditions, coordinate distributed activity, and sustain viability through complex physiological, developmental, and ecological organisation.

Biological Evaluation and Significance can also be recognised without thereby settling cognition. Conditions matter differently to plant viability, and plant organisation responds to those differences.

Some phenomena become more interesting near the cognitive boundary. Stress priming and other temporally extended effects can preserve consequences of earlier conditions and alter later activity. Habituation-like findings may be suggestive. Claims of associative learning remain contested.

But the existence of such phenomena does not remove the comparative burden. The question is whether cognitive explanation adds something that an adequate account of regulation, plasticity, physiological memory, or other non-cognitive organisation does not already explain.

The present Core Plant Cognition article therefore distinguishes pre-cognitive, suggestive, cognitively indeterminate, and potentially positive cases rather than inferring cognition from plant complexity as a whole. In the current assessment, no plant phenomenon considered warrants the strongest positive minimal-cognition classification.

That conclusion belongs to the current Core article and should be evaluated there. The significance of the result for the present synthesis is historical and methodological.

APS can now return a null or indeterminate cognitive attribution while continuing to affirm the Agency, Evaluation, Significance, Integration, and biological importance demonstrated by the underlying phenomena.

The framework therefore no longer requires plant cognition to validate the biological insight with which its plant-cognition programme began.

## 9. What the Plant Case Reveals About APS

The development of APS plant cognition is neither straightforward continuity nor straightforward reversal.

There is continuity in the biological starting point. Agency remains indispensable. Cognition is still approached as a biological phenomenon rather than defined through human capacities, consciousness, or possession of a nervous system. Plant organisation remains scientifically important irrespective of its eventual cognitive classification.

There is differentiation in the conceptual architecture. Life, Agency, Biological Evaluation, Significance, Integration, and Cognition now perform distinguishable explanatory functions. The pathway among them expresses dependencies within one living organisation rather than interchangeable names for increasing complexity.

There is restriction in the cognition boundary. Sophisticated regulation, signalling, integration, temporal retention, and adaptive modulation no longer establish cognition simply by accumulating complexity. Cognitive attribution requires a more discriminating account of how biological significance is organised across time and viability-relevant possibilities.

And there is methodological addition. A coherent APS interpretation is no longer sufficient evidence of explanatory gain. Claims must be attached to specified explananda, tested against adequate comparators, and exposed to outcomes that may be positive, null, adverse, complementary, or unresolved.

Plant cognition brings these developments into unusually clear relation because the biological problem remained recognisable while the framework used to analyse it changed.

That does not show that the 2025 formulation was simply wrong. Nor does it establish that the current formulation is final. A developing research programme may preserve an originating insight while changing the distinctions and evidential requirements through which stronger claims are made.

The important transition is therefore not from taking plants seriously as cognitive organisms to ceasing to take them seriously. It is from asking whether the complexity of plant Agency can support a biologically expanded conception of cognition to asking, phenomenon by phenomenon, whether cognitive explanation provides warranted explanatory gain beyond the strongest adequate account of non-cognitive biological organisation.

This also changes what counts as an informative result.

If a plant phenomenon is adequately explained without cognition, that result helps clarify the boundary between Agency and Cognition. If the evidence remains indeterminate, the uncertainty identifies what additional dependency would need to be demonstrated. If a future case establishes explanatory gain for a cognitive account, APS must be capable of recognising that result without having guaranteed it in advance.

Plant cognition thus remains important to APS for a reason that differs from the role it played at the framework's public beginning. It is no longer only a domain in which a biologically grounded conception of cognition can be extended beyond familiar neural cases. It is also a domain in which the distinctions and comparative controls of APS can be exposed to a demanding test.

The history therefore illustrates a broader feature of the framework's development. Increasing conceptual differentiation does not necessarily produce broader explanatory claims. Stronger methodological controls may instead narrow what can responsibly be asserted. In the plant-cognition case, that narrowing preserves rather than diminishes the underlying biological problem: how living organisation comes to evaluate what matters, integrate significance across changing conditions, and, in some cases, organise that significance across time in ways that warrant the further attribution of cognition.

## 1. The Plant Cognition Problem

Debates over plant cognition have long oscillated between two unsatisfactory poles. At one extreme, cognition is tied so closely to nervous systems, representation, consciousness, or animal-like behaviour that plants are excluded largely by definition. At the other, cognition is extended to adaptive responsiveness, signalling, plasticity, learning-like change, or biological complexity so broadly that the distinction between cognition and regulation becomes difficult to maintain (Alpi et al. 2007; Taiz et al. 2019; Segundo-OrtÃ­n et al. 2025).

Both positions respond to genuine features of biological explanation. Neural systems support forms of integration, learning, representation and behavioural flexibility central to many familiar cases of cognition. Plants, by contrast, lack nervous systems yet display extensive environmental sensitivity, systemic signalling, developmental plasticity, history-dependent regulation and coordinated adjustment to changing conditions. The difficulty arises when either anatomical similarity or adaptive complexity is treated as a sufficient criterion for cognitive attribution.

The plant cognition debate therefore exposes a broader problem:

> A biologically grounded account of cognition must be permissive enough to recognise genuinely non-neural cognitive organisation if it exists, but restrictive enough to distinguish cognition from the sophisticated regulation already required by living systems.

This problem cannot be solved merely by deciding whether plants appear intelligent, whether their behaviour resembles that of animals, or whether particular mechanisms are sufficiently complex. The relevant question is explanatory: **what organisation must be demonstrated before cognitive description contributes something beyond an adequate biological account of regulation, development and adaptation?**

APS approaches the issue from this direction. It does not begin by classifying plants globally as cognitive or non-cognitive. Nor does it infer cognition from viability, biological agency, signalling, learning, temporal extension, or distributed organisation alone. Instead, it asks which specified plant phenomena, if any, warrant cognitive explanation once the strongest adequate non-cognitive account has been considered.

This shifts the debate from taxonomic classification to comparative explanation.

**Where This Article Fits**

*This article applies the APS cognition boundary to the plant-cognition debate. It does not own the general definition or demarcation of cognition, the broader continuity from Life to Mind, or the account of what cognition contributes once cognitive attribution has been warranted.*

*Those questions are developed elsewhere in the APS cognition corpus. The present article has a narrower task: to ask whether specified plant phenomena warrant cognitive explanation relative to adequate non-cognitive comparators.*

*Plants are especially informative for this purpose because they combine sophisticated viability-oriented regulation, distributed sensing, systemic signalling, developmental plasticity and history-sensitive activity without nervous systems. They therefore provide a demanding test of whether cognitive attribution can extend beyond familiar neural cases without collapsing cognition into biological regulation in general.*

## 2. What Counts as Evidence for Plant Cognition?

Plants possess many capacities that are relevant to cognition research without independently establishing cognition.

They detect and discriminate environmental conditions through distributed sensory mechanisms. Electrical, hormonal and chemical signalling can coordinate activity over considerable portions of the organism. Growth and development change in response to light, water, nutrients, mechanical conditions, herbivory and other perturbations. Previous exposure can alter later physiological responses, sometimes over substantial intervals. These phenomena demonstrate complex biological organisation and provide legitimate material for investigating cognition (Sultan 2000; Toyota et al. 2018; Segundo-OrtÃ­n et al. 2025).

But evidence relevant to cognition is not the same as evidence sufficient for cognition.

Environmental sensing establishes discrimination among conditions. Systemic signalling establishes material coordination. Developmental plasticity establishes history-sensitive adjustment. Stress priming establishes that prior perturbation can alter later responsiveness. Learning-like experiments may indicate modification through experience. None of these findings by itself determines whether cognition is required to explain the phenomenon.

The distinction is especially important because living systems are already organised historically. Regulatory networks can retain state. Development can alter later response possibilities. Molecular persistence, epigenetic modification, hormonal state, structural change and altered resource allocation can produce temporally extended effects without requiring cognitive organisation. A plant can therefore exhibit activity that is selective, integrated, adaptive and historically modulated while the relevant dependencies remain adequately explained through biological regulation.

Evidence for plant cognition must consequently do more than establish complexity or temporal persistence. It must discriminate between at least two hypotheses:

1. the phenomenon results from sophisticated but sufficiently fixed biological regulation; or
2. biological significance is organised across time in a way that modulates present activity relative to viability-relevant possibilities beyond what the regulatory account explains.

That distinction places the burden of proof on the organisation itself rather than on the vocabulary.

The comparative test therefore proceeds in four steps: specify the plant phenomenon and explanandum; reconstruct the strongest adequate non-cognitive explanation; ask whether the phenomenon exhibits the organisation required by the provisional APS cognitive boundary; and assign an evidential grade according to whether cognitive explanation is unnecessary, suggestive, unresolved against the comparator, or positively warranted. The test concerns explanatory gain for the specified phenomenon, not the cognitive status of plants as a whole.

## 3. The Strongest Case for Plant Cognition

The strongest case for plant cognition does not depend on claiming that plants possess consciousness, brains, or human-like mental states. **It arises from phenomena in which prior conditions appear to alter later activity in context-sensitive ways.**

Several candidate families are important.

### Stress Priming

Plant stress priming is particularly significant because exposure to a non-lethal perturbation can alter responses to later stress. Drought or dehydration priming can produce persistent physiological and developmental changes that alter later stress responsiveness (Bruce et al. 2007).

This makes priming more than an instantaneous stimulus-response relation. Earlier conditions continue to influence later organisation, and those effects can matter to viability.

### Habituation-Like Response Modification

Some plant experiments have been interpreted as demonstrating habituation or memory-like modification through repeated exposure (Gagliano et al. 2014). If a plant becomes selectively less responsive to a recurrent non-harmful stimulus while retaining responsiveness to other significant conditions, this would be relevant to a cognition boundary because history would be affecting present significance.

The explanatory issue, however, is whether the phenomenon reflects flexible organisation of retained significance or physiological adaptation, fatigue, altered thresholding, or some other non-cognitive mechanism.

### Associative-Learning Claims

The strongest plant-learning claims attempt to go further by showing that a previously neutral cue can acquire behavioural significance through association with another condition. Gagliano et al. (2016), for example, reported conditioning-like effects in pea seedlings in which fan position was associated with subsequent light location.

If reproducible, such a phenomenon would be important. A neutral condition would apparently acquire altered significance through its relation to another outcome, and that acquired relation would later modulate growth.

But this case is also methodologically contested. Markel (2020) reported no evidence of the associative-learning effect in an attempted replication of the pea paradigm. Subsequent analysis has emphasised methodological differences and the need for improved comparative experimental protocols rather than treating either the original claim or its rejection as automatically decisive (Ponkshe et al. 2024).

The strongest case for plant cognition therefore exists not in generic claims about intelligence but in specific phenomena involving retained significance, changed cue relations, context-dependent deployment and consequence-sensitive modification.

The central question is whether those relations are actually demonstrated.

## 4. The Strongest Non-Cognitive Explanation

A fair cognitive interpretation must be compared with the strongest available biological alternative rather than with a simplistic model of plants as passive stimulus-response machines.

Plants possess sophisticated non-cognitive mechanisms capable of generating many of the phenomena used to motivate cognitive language.

Prior stress, for example, can produce persistent physiological and developmental changes that alter later responsiveness. A later stress can therefore produce a different response because the organism is materially different from the unprimed plant (Bruce et al. 2007).

Nothing in such an explanation requires that the plant represent future drought, evaluate alternative hypothetical worlds, or cognitively retrieve a memory. The earlier perturbation has changed the regulatory organisation that encounters the later one.

Developmental plasticity provides a related comparator. Plants can alter morphology, growth allocation and other developmental outcomes as environmental conditions change (Sultan 2000). Such organisation is temporally extended and may be adaptive, context-sensitive and consequential for viability. Yet developmental regulation can remain governed by evolved conditional relations without requiring a separate cognitive explanation.

Systemic signalling presents another important control. Long-distance calcium signalling can coordinate local events across plant tissues during defence responses (Toyota et al. 2018). This establishes that organism-wide coordination need not depend upon a central nervous system. It does not establish that the organisation is cognitive.

The strongest non-cognitive explanation of stress priming can therefore be stated as follows:

> Earlier stress produces persistent physiological and developmental changes that alter later activity through evolved regulatory relations. The organism is history-sensitive and may be functionally prepared for recurrent conditions, but its activity need not involve contextual reorganisation of significance among alternatives.

This comparator is not a residual explanation used only when cognition fails. It is a serious biological account that cognitive explanation must outperform.

APS should therefore agree with sceptical interpretations whenever fixed or conditionally regulated physiological organisation adequately explains the phenomenon. Cognitive terminology adds no explanatory gain merely because regulation is distributed, adaptive, anticipatory in function, or extended through time.

## 5. The APS Cognitive Boundary

APS distinguishes the biological foundations of cognition from cognition itself.

Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation. Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity. Through Biological Evaluation, differences acquire significance relative to the maintenance and re-establishment of the organism's continued functioning.

Plants clearly satisfy these pre-cognitive conditions. Water availability, tissue damage, nutrient conditions, light, temperature and other environmental relations matter because they alter the conditions under which plant organisation can persist. Plant activity is therefore normatively structured in the biological sense: some trajectories better sustain viability than others.

APS expresses this explanatory dependency as:

Biological Agency â†’ Biological Evaluation â†’ Significance â†’ Integration â†’ Cognition

The sequence is not a hierarchy, chronology, or set of independent components. It identifies explanatory dependencies.

Most importantly, the earlier terms do not entail the later one.

Biological significance can exist without cognition. A plant can evaluate conditions in the APS senseâ€”that is, its viability-oriented organisation can generate differential significanceâ€”without cognitively organising those conditions. Integration also does not settle the issue. Living systems necessarily coordinate multiple processes, and highly integrated regulation may remain non-cognitive.

Biological significance is central because it provides the content of minimal cognition: cognition does not introduce a new source of what matters biologically, but organises what already matters for viability across time.

The canonical APS definition is:

Cognition is the organisation of biological significance across time.

The current APS boundary proposal adds a provisional attribution criterion:

Biological agency becomes cognitive when integrated biological significance modulates activity across a temporal field of viability-relevant possibilities in ways not exhausted by immediate or fixed regulation.

Put more simply, biological agency counts as cognitive when the system organises what matters for its viability across time in relation to relevant possibilities, in ways that modulate present activity and cannot be adequately explained by immediate cues or fixed regulatory routines.

This is not a second definition of cognition. It is a testable proposal about the point at which cognitive attribution becomes justified.

The distinction is decisive for plants. Stress responses, signalling networks, developmental plasticity and temporal retention may establish Biological Agency, Biological Evaluation, Significance and Integration without crossing the proposed cognitive boundary.

The plant question is therefore not whether plants have biological significance. They plainly do within APS. The question is whether some plant phenomena organise that significance across time in the stronger sense identified by the provisional boundary.

## 6. Plant Phenomena Against the Boundary

### 6.1 Stress Priming: The Central Borderline Case

Recurrent drought or dehydration priming provides the strongest current plant case for testing the APS boundary.

It satisfies several important conditions.

- First, the phenomenon is viability related. Water deficit materially affects continued plant functioning.

- Second, it includes retention. Earlier conditions alter later organisation after the original perturbation has ended.

- Third, it can involve distributed integration. Later changes may be expressed through multiple physiological and developmental processes.

- Fourth, primed and unprimed plants can respond differently to later stress.

These properties make stress priming significantly richer than immediate physiological regulation.

They do not, however, establish cognition.

A retained molecular, physiological or developmental state can directly modify later response. Temporal displacement therefore does not necessarily demonstrate cognitive temporal organisation. Likewise, the fact that priming prepares a plant for recurrent stress establishes functional preparation, not necessarily cognitive anticipation.

The distinction can be sharpened experimentally.

Suppose drought priming is first established. Some plants then encounter recurrent drought, under which retaining the primed state remains beneficial. Others encounter prolonged favourable conditions under which continued priming is costly. The relation between prior conditions and later consequences can subsequently be altered and later restored.

The critical question is whether deployment of the primed response changes according to the changed consequences.

If the response simply persists, decays, or resets according to fixed regulatory dynamics, the non-cognitive interpretation remains sufficient.

If the organism can modify how the retained relation mattersâ€”reducing, reversing and later reacquiring the response as its consequences changeâ€”then the phenomenon would provide stronger evidence of cognitive organisation.

The present evidence does not yet establish this distinction clearly enough.

Stress priming should therefore be classified as:

**Grade 2 â€” cognitively indeterminate.**

This classification is substantive. It means that sophisticated temporally extended biological organisation is well supported, while cognitive and non-cognitive explanations remain insufficiently discriminated.

### 6.2 Associative-Learning Claims: Suggestive but Contested

Pea associative-learning experiments potentially address the missing discriminator more directly.

If a physically neutral cue genuinely acquires altered significance through association with a later outcome, and the plant subsequently uses that acquired relation to modulate growth, the case would provide evidence beyond simple environmental responsiveness (Gagliano et al. 2016).

But the empirical foundation is not currently secure enough to carry a positive cognitive verdict.

Markel (2020) reported no evidence of the associative-learning effect in an attempted replication of the pea paradigm, while subsequent analysis has emphasised methodological differences and the need for improved experimental discrimination (Ponkshe et al. 2024).

Under APS this receives:

**Grade 1 â€” suggestive, empirically contested.**

The case remains theoretically important because robust evidence under strong controls could move plant evidence closer to the cognitive boundary. It cannot currently function as the foundation for a general claim that plants are cognitive.

### 6.3 Habituation-Like Learning

Habituation-like effects are also potentially relevant because they concern the modification of present response by previous experience (Gagliano et al. 2014).

But apparent habituation must be distinguished from physiological adaptation, fatigue, depletion, fixed threshold change and other non-cognitive mechanisms.

Existing evidence therefore supports treating such phenomena as **suggestive candidates**, not as established cognition.

### 6.4 Developmental Plasticity, Sensing and Systemic Signalling

Developmental plasticity, distributed sensing and whole-plant signalling remain important to the analysis but have a different evidential role.

They demonstrate that plants possess:

- viability-oriented agency;
- Biological Evaluation;
- biological significance;
- material integration;
- temporally extended organisation.

These properties provide biological conditions within which cognition could occur.

They do not independently show that it does.

Accordingly, generic developmental plasticity and systemic sensing or signalling should function principally as pre-cognitive baselines and non-cognitive comparators rather than as positive cognition criteria (Sultan 2000; Toyota et al. 2018).

## 7. Evidence Grades and Case Verdicts

The plant evidence can now be differentiated rather than aggregated into a single global judgement.

The evidential grades distinguish outcomes of the comparative test rather than degrees of biological complexity. Grade 0 identifies phenomena adequately explained by non-cognitive biological organisation. Grade 1 â€” suggestive identifies cognition-relevant evidence that does not yet establish a genuine cognitive boundary case. Grade 2 â€” cognitively indeterminate identifies a genuine boundary case in which cognitive and adequate non-cognitive explanations have not yet been sufficiently discriminated. Grade 3 â€” minimal-cognitive positive identifies a phenomenon for which the evidence warrants cognitive attribution relative to the specified explanandum and comparator. These grades apply to phenomena, not organisms.

<div class="aps-diagram">
  <a href="/assets/diagrams/table-plant-cognition.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener">
    <img
      src="/assets/diagrams/table-plant-cognition.png"
      alt="Table summarising the APS evidential status of candidate plant cognition phenomena, from pre-cognitive sensing and signalling to cognitively indeterminate stress priming and suggestive learning claims."
      loading="lazy"
    />
  </a>
</div>

No plant phenomenon considered here presently warrants **Grade 3 â€” minimal-cognitive positive**.

That conclusion should not be interpreted as evidence that plants are intrinsically non-cognitive. It establishes only that the present evidence does not yet discriminate cognitive organisation from adequate non-cognitive explanation strongly enough.

Equally, Grade 2 should not be treated as a rhetorical compromise. It identifies the missing evidence.

For stress priming, stronger cognitive warrant would require evidence of relations such as:

- contextual redeployment of retained significance;
- consequence-sensitive updating;
- cueâ€“consequence reversal;
- reacquisition after reversal;
- significant generalisation or discrimination;
- organism-level integration of those changes.

These are experimentally addressable questions.

The evidential grades also apply to **phenomena rather than organisms**. A particular plant may exhibit ordinary regulation in one context and a stronger candidate phenomenon in another. Even a future Grade 3 result would initially justify cognitive attribution relative to that phenomenon, not automatically to every activity of the species or to plants generally.

## 8. What Plant Cognition Wouldâ€”and Would Notâ€”Show

If a plant phenomenon eventually satisfies the cognitive boundary, several conclusions would follow.

- First, cognition would not be restricted in principle to nervous systems. Neural tissue would remain a powerful implementation of cognition rather than a constitutive requirement.

- Second, a positive plant case would support organisational rather than taxonomic classification. Cognitive status would depend on how biological significance is organised, not on whether the organism belongs to a familiar cognitive lineage.

- Third, a positive case would reinforce the distinction between cognition and consciousness. Nothing in the minimal boundary requires phenomenal awareness.

- Fourth, plant cognition would not automatically entail representation. APS remains neutral concerning representational explanation at the minimal boundary. Representation may be useful or required for particular phenomena, but it should not be assumed simply because cognition is attributed.

- Fifth, a positive result would not show that all living systems are cognitive. On the contrary, the possibility of demonstrating a plant case would depend upon maintaining a meaningful distinction between cognition and the Biological Agency, Biological Evaluation, Significance and Integration already present more widely in life.

Conversely, failure to establish cognition in current plant cases would not diminish plant agency. Plants remain viability-oriented, evaluative living organisations regardless of the outcome of the cognitive debate.

This point is especially important. Cognitive vocabulary should not function as a measure of biological importance or organisational sophistication. A non-cognitive plant is not thereby passive, mechanistically trivial, or biologically deficient.

## 9. Implications for Minimal Cognition and Biological Explanation

The plant case is valuable precisely because it resists easy classification.

Much discussion of minimal cognition begins with rapidly moving organisms, behavioural choice or paradigms derived from animal learning. Plants organise activity differently. Growth, physiology, distributed signalling, resource allocation and development unfold over different spatial and temporal extents.

A viable criterion for minimal cognition must therefore be applicable without importing locomotion, nervous systems, rapid decision-making or animal-specific behavioural paradigms as hidden requirements.

At the same time, adapting cognitive tests to plant organisation cannot mean weakening the boundary until all adaptive plasticity qualifies.

Plant stress priming makes this methodological problem particularly clear.

It shows that:

- temporal extension is not cognition;
- memory terminology is not cognitive memory;
- functional preparation is not cognitive anticipation;
- multiple physiological possibilities are not automatically cognitively organised alternatives;
- organism-wide signalling is not cognition;
- material integration is necessary to many biological explanations without being cognitively diagnostic.

The plant case therefore provides a demanding test of the APS proposal.

If experiments demonstrate that retained significance can be contextually redeployed and updated as its consequences change, plant priming could move from sophisticated regulation toward minimal cognition.

If fixed molecular, physiological and developmental relations continue to explain the results adequately, cognitive attribution should be withheld.

If the evidence remains unable to distinguish these alternatives, indeterminacy is the appropriate scientific outcome.

This is also a test of APS itself.

A comparative explanatory methodology should not guarantee the preferred attribution. It should identify what would count against it. If plant cognition can be asserted whenever signalling, history dependence or adaptive coordination is found, APS would add little to the existing debate. Its value lies instead in specifying what further evidence would be required and accepting a null or indeterminate result when that evidence is absent.

The plant cognition problem therefore becomes more scientifically productive once the answer is no longer built into the framework.

## 10. Conclusion

The plant cognition debate cannot be resolved by choosing between neural exclusivity and unrestricted cognitive extension. Plants plainly exhibit rich biological agency: they sense environmental conditions, coordinate activity through distributed signalling, alter development and physiology under changing conditions, retain effects of prior perturbation, and generate biological significance relative to viability. Within APS, none of these capacities by itself establishes cognition.

The cognitive question begins only after these pre-cognitive capacities are acknowledged.

Cognition is the organisation of biological significance across time. The current APS boundary proposal holds that **biological agency becomes cognitive when integrated biological significance modulates activity across a temporal field of viability-relevant possibilities in ways not exhausted by immediate or fixed regulation.** Put more simply, cognition becomes a candidate explanation when what matters to an organism because of past or possible conditions modulates its present activity in ways that an adequate account of immediate cues or fixed regulatory routines cannot explain.

This distinction is crucial in the plant case. A drought-primed plant may respond differently to a later drought because the earlier event produced persistent molecular, physiological or developmental changes. Temporal retention and altered later activity are therefore not sufficient for cognitive attribution. A stronger cognitive case would require evidence that retained biological significance is deployed differently as circumstances and their viability consequences change, in ways not adequately explained by such regulatory persistence.

Applied to the present evidence, the APS boundary therefore produces a differentiated rather than a global verdict. Distributed sensing, systemic signalling and developmental plasticity demonstrate sophisticated biological organisation but do not independently warrant cognition. Stress priming provides a stronger boundary case because prior viability-relevant conditions can alter later organismal activity after the original perturbation has ceased. Yet temporally extended molecular, physiological and developmental regulation remains an adequate explanation for much of the available evidence. Stress priming is therefore cognitively indeterminate.

Habituation-like response modification provides suggestive evidence but is not decisive. Associative-learning claims would provide stronger evidence if robustly established, but their current empirical status remains contested. None of the principal plant phenomena considered here therefore presently warrants a Grade 3 minimal-cognitive-positive classification.

The current evidence consequently supports neither a global attribution of minimal cognition to plants nor the conclusion that plant cognition is impossible. Plants instead occupy an important methodological position: they provide a demanding test of whether cognitive explanation can extend beyond nervous systems without collapsing cognition into biological regulation in general.

This is the productive outcome of the plant cognition debate. The relevant question is no longer whether plants should be classified as cognitive because they are complex, adaptive, responsive or biologically impressive. It is whether specified plant phenomena organise biological significance across time in ways for which cognitive explanation provides explanatory gain over the strongest adequate non-cognitive account.

For the principal cases presently available, that question remains open.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

Do specified plant phenomena warrant cognitive explanation when tested against the APS cognition boundary and the strongest adequate non-cognitive comparators?

### Architectural Role

This article is the principal APS domain-specific application of the cognition boundary to plants. It examines whether sophisticated plant regulation crosses from pre-cognitive biological organisation into cognition without assuming either neural exclusivity or universal plant cognition.

### Builds On

The article builds on the APS accounts of Life, Biological Agency, Biological Evaluation, Significance, Integration and Cognition. It takes as given the canonical definition of cognition as the organisation of biological significance across time and uses the current provisional cognitive-boundary proposal as an attribution criterion rather than as a second definition.

### Develops Into

The analysis develops into comparative adjudication of specified plant phenomena. Stress priming functions as the principal cognitively indeterminate boundary case; habituation-like response modification and pea associative-learning claims provide stronger but currently suggestive or contested cases. These results contribute to the wider empirical testing of minimal cognition without determining the cognitive status of plants as a taxonomic group.

### Related Explanatory Questions

The article connects directly with questions about where cognition belongs in biology, what distinguishes cognition from sophisticated regulation, how cognitive organisation contributes to living activity once warranted, and how non-neural candidate cases should be tested. It does not attempt to resolve Mind, Consciousness, Intelligence or Representation as independent explanatory problems.

### Position within APS

Plant Cognition is a Core article within the cognition-and-mind cluster. Agency, Process and Scale remain complementary analytic projections of one viability-oriented, constraint-closed living organisation rather than independent causes, components or hierarchical levels. The article applies APS comparatively: cognitive attribution is relative to a specified explanandum, relevant materially implemented dependencies and an adequate non-cognitive comparator.

### Corpus Significance

The article provides a stringent test of APS's ability to discriminate rather than merely extend cognitive terminology. Its present result is deliberately asymmetric: plant agency, Biological Evaluation and Significance are robust; stress priming remains cognitively indeterminate; stronger learning claims remain suggestive or contested; and no plant-wide cognitive verdict follows. The article therefore demonstrates that APS can preserve non-neural cognitive possibility while accepting null and indeterminate outcomes where explanatory gain has not been established.
