## Scale â€” How Life Is Coordinated Across Space and Time

> **Where this article fits:** This Core article establishes the meaning and explanatory role of Scale within APS. Scale asks where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents. It does not introduce an additional biological mechanism, causal level, or component of living organisation. Material spatial relations can themselves contribute constitutively to biological organisation; Material spatial relations can themselves contribute constitutively to biological organisation; Scale provides the analytic projection through which the spatial and temporal extent of that organisation becomes the target of analysis.

## Introduction

Biological organisation is materially realised across space and time. Molecules interact within cells; cellular structures occupy particular positions and orientations; cells form tissues whose organisation depends upon boundaries, geometries, local environments, and material relations. Organisms, in turn, maintain their activity through processes distributed across different spatial extents and temporal durations. Biology often describes such differences using terms such as level, hierarchy, size, resolution, or scale. These descriptions can be useful, but they do not by themselves explain how living organisation persists.

APS uses **Scale** in a more specific explanatory sense:

**Scale is the analytic projection concerned with where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.**

Scale therefore does not designate a separate entity or causal domain within a living system, nor is it simply another name for spatial structure. The explanatory object remains one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation. Scale makes explicit the spatial and temporal extents across which the organisation relevant to a particular biological explanandum is materially realised and maintained.

## Scale Beyond Levels

Biology frequently organises phenomena into familiar domains such as molecular, cellular, tissue, organismal, population, ecological, and evolutionary, and nothing in APS requires abandoning those descriptions. The difficulty arises when descriptive divisions are treated as though they were independently acting causal levels, or when assigning a phenomenon to a level is taken to explain it. A molecule does not act because it belongs to a molecular level, a cell does not regulate because it occupies a cellular level, and an organism does not persist because organismal organisation occupies a higher position in a hierarchy. In each case, the relevant causal interactions are materially realised interactions among processes, structures, constraints, and environmental conditions.

These relations can extend across spatial and temporal extents that do not correspond neatly to a single conventional level. APS therefore does not replace one hierarchy with another hierarchy called Scale. Instead, Scale asks:

**Across what spatial and temporal extents is the organisation relevant to this explanandum actually realised?**

This shifts explanatory attention from a presumed ordering of levels toward the organisation that must be identified in the biological case itself.

Conventional level descriptions can distinguish molecular, cellular, organismal, ecological, and evolutionary domains, but these labels do not themselves identify causal organisation. Scale is therefore an analytic projection of living organisation rather than an additional causal layer; organised persistence may be one explanatory target of Scale analysis.

## Scale as an Analytic Projection

Scale does not itself organise biological activity; living systems do. Their organisation is materially realised through processes, structures, boundaries, constraints, interactions, and environmental relations extending through space and time. Scale identifies the analytic projection through which the extent of that organisation is investigated. This distinction matters because statements such as â€œScale coordinates activityâ€ or â€œcausation operates between scalesâ€ can inadvertently turn an analytic distinction into a causal entity. The philosophical status of this distinction is developed in [Living Reality and Biological Explanation â€” What Does APS Mean by an Analytic Projection?](/articles/what-does-aps-mean-by-an-analytic-projection/). That article explains how Scale can direct an investigator-selected explanatory question toward materially real spatial and temporal organisation without turning Scale itself into a biological level, causal domain, or division of reality.

APS instead asks what materially implemented relations alter the conditions under which local activity occurs, how those relations are maintained, and across what spatial and temporal extents the resulting organisation must be analysed. A physiological process, for example, may depend upon molecular reactions, cellular organisation, tissue architecture, vascular relations, neural regulation, and organismâ€“environment interaction. The explanatory task is not completed by saying that these processes occur at different scales; it requires identifying the organisation through which those materially realised relations contribute to continued functioning.

Scale tells us **where that organisation must be sought and delimited**.

## Spatial Structure and Scale

The distinction between **spatial structure** and **Scale** is especially important. Hermida and Ladyman (2026) argue that biological organisation often consists in, or depends upon, spatial structure together with physical interactions among the parts of biological systems. Spatial features such as position, configuration, shape, directionality, orientation, boundaries, and location can therefore matter directly to biological organisation. APS does not redescribe these material spatial relations as Scale. A membrane boundary, the orientation of a cellular structure, the position of a signalling component, or the geometry of a tissue can contribute materially to what a biological system does; those relations belong to the organisation being explained.

**Scale is the analytic projection under which we ask where that organisation is realised across spatial and temporal extents.**

The distinction can therefore be stated simply:

**Spatial organisation concerns materially realised biological relations. Scale concerns the explanatory identification of the extents across which organised persistence is realised.**

The two are closely related, but they are not interchangeable. Recognising the constitutive importance of spatial structure also does not require APS to make a general claim against physical or partâ€“whole explanation. Hermida and Ladyman explicitly distinguish their criticism of genetic and molecular reductionism from physical and suitably spatially informed partâ€“whole explanation, and APS is compatible with that methodological caution. Its concern is not to establish Scale as a rival to physical, mechanistic, spatial, or compositional explanation, but to clarify what must be specified when the organisation relevant to persistence extends beyond the boundaries assumed by a more local description.

## Coordination Across Spatial and Temporal Extents

Living organisation often depends upon relations realised across more than one spatial or temporal extent. Molecular processes operate within cellular structures, cellular activity occurs within tissue organisation, and physiological regulation depends upon materially realised relations distributed through an organism. Organismal activity likewise modifies and is modified by environmental conditions. None of these statements requires scales themselves to interact: the causal work is performed by the materially realised processes and constraints.

A wider organisational arrangement can alter local conditions because that arrangement is implemented through material relations that constrain the possibilities available to local activity. Conversely, local processes can modify the material organisation within which other processes occur. APS therefore avoids treating cross-scale influence as causation exercised by one level over another. The explanatory question is instead:

**Which materially realised relations connect the relevant activities, and across what spatial and temporal extents must those relations be followed to explain continued organisation?**

Persistence may depend upon such distributed coordination, but the coordination belongs to the living organisation. Scale identifies where that organisation is distributed.

## Homeorhesis and Organised Persistence

Living organisation is not maintained by preserving an unchanged state. Material components turn over, structures change, development alters form, environmental conditions vary, and regulatory relations are repeatedly maintained, modified, and re-established. Homeorhesis can describe this persistence through an organised trajectory rather than through static constancy.

Scale does not provide the continuity of such a trajectory. Rather, it asks across what spatial and temporal extents the materially realised organisation underlying that continuity must be tracked. A trajectory may therefore require explanation over seconds or years, within a cell or across an organism, depending upon the explanandum. What persists is the organisation; Scale identifies the extent over which that persistence is organised.

## Scale and the APS Triad

Scale is one of three analytic projections through which APS organises biological explanation:

- **Agency** concerns what living systems do.
- **Process** concerns how continuity is maintained despite change.
- **Scale** concerns where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.

These are **analytic projections rather than components of reality**. They are not three independent mechanisms, three stages through which living systems pass, or biological levels, and persistence does not arise from their interaction. The explanatory object is one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation: Agency makes its activity explicit, Process makes its continuity through change explicit, and Scale makes the spatial and temporal extent of its organised persistence explicit.

The three projections can therefore place different explanatory questions before the same biological case without dividing the living organisation into separate ontological dimensions.

## Scale-Indexed Organisation

Biological properties cannot automatically be transferred from one spatial or temporal extent to another. Evidence that a local process contributes to regulation does not establish that a larger aggregate is itself an agent; evidence that components exchange information does not establish cognition at every encompassing domain; and the persistence of an ecological or evolutionary pattern does not automatically establish that the ecological system, species, or lineage possesses the same organisational properties as a living organism.

Scale therefore performs an important discriminatory role in explanation. Claims must be warranted for the organisation to which they are attributed and for the spatial and temporal extent over which that organisation is materially realised. This is particularly important for concepts such as:

- biological agency
- normativity
- cognition
- semiosis
- individuality
- and organised persistence

Similarity across domains can justify comparison, but it does not by itself establish identity of biological organisation. Scale analysis therefore helps prevent the uncritical projection of explanatory concepts from one domain or extent to another.

## Why Scale Matters

Scale matters because biological explananda frequently depend upon organisation whose relevant boundaries cannot be assumed in advance. A local mechanism may be sufficient for one question, while another may require relations extending across cells, tissues, an organism, or organismâ€“environment coupling. Still other questions concern developmental, ecological, or evolutionary phenomena whose spatial and temporal extents differ from those of organismal self-maintenance.

APS does not assume that every biological explanation must encompass the widest available extent, nor does it presume that a broader description is intrinsically more explanatory than a local one. The relevant extent is determined by the explanandum and by the materially realised dependencies required to explain it. Scale therefore helps clarify:

- why conventional level labels do not by themselves supply explanations;
- where the organisation relevant to an explanandum is materially realised;
- when a more local or more extended explanatory domain is required;
- how spatial and temporal organisation contribute to biological persistence;
- and why biological properties must be attributed only where the relevant organisation is established.

Scale is therefore **target-sensitive**. More Scale is not more explanation; the relevant Scale is the spatial and temporal extent required by the explanatory target.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

**Where is the organisation relevant to biological persistence realised across spatial and temporal extents, and what explanatory difference does identifying those extents make?**

### Architectural Role

This Core article establishes the APS meaning of **Scale**:

**Scale is the analytic projection concerned with where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.**

It does not constitute a biological mechanism, causal level, spatial structure, or independent organisational dimension. The material organisation identified under a Scale analysis may include boundaries, configurations, spatial relations, constraints, interactions, trajectories, and environmental couplings. Those relations belong to the biological system or explanandum under investigation; Scale identifies their relevant explanatory extent.

### Spatial-Organisation Comparator

Hermida and Ladyman (2026) provide an important contemporary comparator because they defend the constitutive explanatory importance of spatial structure in biology, but their account and APS Scale are not identical proposals. Hermida and Ladyman address how material spatial organisation contributes to biological phenomena; APS Scale asks where persistence-relevant organisation is realised across spatial and temporal extents.

Where these approaches address the same explanatory target, APS does not assume an additional explanatory contribution merely by redescribing the phenomenon in Scale terminology. Any claimed explanatory gain requires target-matched comparison with the strongest established account of that target.

### Position Within APS

Scale must be understood together with Agency and Process without being converted into an independently acting component of living organisation.

**Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation.**

Agency concerns what that organisation does, Process concerns how its continuity is maintained despite change, and Scale concerns where that persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents. These projections can be distinguished analytically because different biological questions give different explanatory priority to activity, continuity, or extent; they nevertheless concern the same materially realised organisation.

## Conclusion

Scale is not size, hierarchy, or an independently acting biological level, nor is it identical to spatial structure. Material spatial relations can contribute constitutively to biological organisation: boundaries, positions, configurations, orientations, shapes, constraints, and physical interactions can all matter to how living systems function and persist. APS Scale asks a different but complementary explanatory question:

**Where is the organisation through which persistence is maintained realised across spatial and temporal extents?**

The answer must be established from the biological case rather than imposed by a predetermined hierarchy. Living organisation performs the causal and coordinative work; Scale makes its relevant extent explicit. Within APS, Scale therefore remains an analytic projection of one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation: the projection concerned with **where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents**.

# Scale, Time, and Persistence â€” Why Life Exists Only Through Organised Continuity

> **Where this article fits:** This Synthesis article brings together organised persistence, temporal continuity, and the APS analytic projection of Scale. It does not redefine Scale or treat time and Scale as additional components of living organisation. The Core Scale article establishes Scale as the analytic projection concerned with where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents. The present article asks how that explanatory perspective contributes to understanding living systems whose organisation continues through material and temporal change.

## Persistence as Organised Continuity

Living systems exist through continuity, but biological continuity does not mean remaining materially unchanged. Cells replace components, molecules are synthesised and degraded, structures are repaired and remodelled, and physiological conditions fluctuate as organisms develop, act, and respond to changing environments. The material composition of a living system can therefore change substantially while its organisation continues.

APS describes the explanatory problem posed by this continuity as **organised persistence**. Persistence is neither simply the continued presence of matter nor passive resistance to change. It is the continuing maintenance and re-establishment of the organisation through which a living system remains viable despite ongoing material transformation. The central explanatory question is therefore not merely what remains unchanged, but **how living organisation is maintained and re-established through change**. This places continuity itself among the principal targets of biological explanation.

## Time as Organised Continuity

Living organisation is necessarily enacted through time. A static description can identify structures, components, concentrations, boundaries, or relations at a particular moment, and such descriptions may be indispensable, but living organisation cannot be exhausted by a succession of static states. Metabolic activity continues, constraints are maintained or regenerated, damage is repaired, and regulatory relations modify activity as conditions change. Development likewise transforms organisation while preserving sufficient continuity for the developing system to remain viable.

Time matters, then, because persistence is temporally extended activity, not because time acts as an independent biological cause. It is the organism's materially realised activity that maintains and re-establishes its organisation through time. Temporal analysis makes this continuity and transformation explicit without turning time itself into the source of biological organisation.

## Scale and the Extent of Organised Persistence

Temporal continuity alone does not determine where the organisation relevant to persistence is realised. Depending upon the explanandum, biological explanation may require molecular interactions within a local cellular region, relations distributed across tissues and organs, organism-wide regulation, organismâ€“environment coupling, or processes extending over developmental or evolutionary durations. APS addresses this question of explanatory extent through **Scale**.

**Scale is the analytic projection concerned with where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.**

Scale does not coordinate the processes through which persistence is maintained, nor does it integrate molecular, cellular, physiological, developmental, ecological, or evolutionary processes into a biological whole. Living organisation performs the relevant causal and coordinative work. Where integration occurs, it must be materially realised through actual biological relationsâ€”interactions, constraints, structures, boundaries, regulatory processes, environmental conditions, or other dependencies established in the biological case. Scale identifies the spatial and temporal extent over which those relations must be followed when they matter to the explanandum. In this way, an explanatory perspective is kept distinct from the biological mechanisms and relations being explained.

## Spatial Organisation and Explanatory Scale

Spatial organisation can itself contribute materially to biological organisation. Hermida and Ladyman (2026) emphasise that position, configuration, shape, orientation, directionality, boundaries, and physical relations among biological parts can be constitutively important to biological phenomena. APS accepts the importance of such spatial organisation without identifying it with Scale.

A membrane boundary can materially constrain interaction, the location of a signalling component can affect what it does, tissue geometry can alter physiological possibilities, and the spatial arrangement of cells can contribute directly to development or function. These are properties and relations of the materially realised organisation itself. Scale asks a different question: across what spatial and temporal extents must that organisation be identified in order to explain the persistence-relevant phenomenon under investigation?

Material spatial organisation and explanatory Scale are therefore related but distinct. Spatial organisation belongs to the biological organisation being explained; Scale identifies the analytic perspective from which the relevant extent of that organisation becomes explicit.

## Persistence Across Differing Extents

Living systems depend upon activities whose characteristic spatial and temporal extents differ substantially. Molecular interactions may occur rapidly and locally, cellular organisation may be maintained across longer durations and larger spatial regions, and physiological regulation may depend upon relations distributed throughout an organism. Development extends organised transformation across substantial portions of a lifetime, while organismâ€“environment relations may persist or recur over still different durations and spatial extents.

These differences imply neither a hierarchy of increasingly important biological levels nor processes belonging to independently acting scales. They show instead that the organisation relevant to a biological explanation may have to be traced across different extents. A local account can be sufficient when the explanandum is local and the relevant dependencies are adequately captured within that boundary. A more extended account becomes necessary only when the explanandum depends upon organisation that the local description does not adequately represent.

Scale is therefore target-sensitive. **The widest explanation is not automatically the best explanation.** The relevant extent is determined by the organisation required to explain the biological target.

## Viability Through Time

Organised persistence is viability-relative. A living system does not merely undergo change; its organisation maintains and re-establishes conditions under which continued functioning remains possible. Biological continuity therefore differs from the persistence of an inert structure. A rock can remain physically present without actively maintaining the conditions of its own existence, whereas a living system continually participates in maintaining the organisation upon which its continued activity depends.

Within APS:

**Life is viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation.**

This organisation consists in the ongoing modulation of constraints through which a system actively maintains and re-establishes the conditions of its own persistence. Persistence concerns the continuation of this organisation through time, while Scale asks where that persistence-relevant organisation is realised. Neither viability nor persistence is thereby distributed automatically across every domain connected to a living system. Claims about viability, agency, normativity, or persistence must remain indexed to the organisation for which the relevant relations are established.

## Persistence as Organisational Achievement

The persistence of a living system is an achievement of organisation rather than the conservation of a fixed material state, a point that becomes particularly clear under perturbation. A living system can be displaced from an existing condition and nevertheless continue because its organisation modifies activity, repairs damage, restores constraints, reorganises relations, or establishes a new viable trajectory. Continuity can therefore be maintained through substantial transformation rather than through the preservation of an invariant state.

Homeorhesis captures an important aspect of this phenomenon by describing persistence in terms of an organised trajectory rather than repeated return to a fixed condition. APS places this insight within the broader problem of organised persistence. The explanatory target is not an abstract trajectory by itself but the materially realised organisation through which viable continuity is maintained despite transformation. Temporal analysis makes continuity through change explicit; Scale identifies the spatial and temporal extent across which the relevant organisation must be followed.

## Scale, Time, and Biological Significance

The relationship between Scale and time also matters when biological activity acquires significance for the living system. A change matters biologically because of its relation to viability, and the same environmental event can therefore have different consequences depending upon the organisation of the system, its current condition, its history, and the temporal possibilities opened or closed by that event. Biological significance need not, for this reason, be confined to an instantaneous local interaction.

In organisms capable of integrating biological significance across time, present activity can be modulated in relation to temporally extended viability-relevant possibilities. This does not mean that Scale produces significance or cognition, nor does temporal extension by itself establish cognition. Scale instead helps delimit where the materially realised organisation relevant to the explanandum must be located. The explanatory requirements for agency, biological evaluation, cognition, and other organisational capacities must then be established independently rather than inferred merely from spatial or temporal extension.

## Developmental, Ecological, and Evolutionary Continuity

Developmental, ecological, and evolutionary phenomena introduce explanatory targets extending beyond many immediate physiological processes. Development concerns organised transformation through an individual lifetime, ecological explanation can require organismâ€“environment relations extending beyond organismal boundaries, and evolution concerns historical transformation across generations. These phenomena should not be collapsed into a single multiscale causal process, because their explananda and characteristic temporal extents differ and the biological organisation relevant to each must be established independently.

APS therefore does not infer that an ecological system or evolutionary lineage possesses the same viability-oriented organisation as an organism merely because organismal persistence depends upon environmental or historical relations. Nor does the existence of long-duration processes establish a wider agent encompassing the organisms involved. Scale instead asks:

**Where is the organisation relevant to this particular explanandum realised, and across what spatial and temporal extents must it be followed?**

This question allows developmental, ecological, and evolutionary relations to enter explanation where they are materially relevant without transferring organismal properties to wider domains without evidence.

## Multiscale Temporality

Biological processes occur over markedly different temporal durations and spatial extents, and representing those differences can be useful when it clarifies the organisation relevant to an explanandum. Such representations should not, however, be interpreted as depicting independently acting biological scales, nor should arrows among domains be taken to mean that Scale itself mediates causal influence. The causal relations remain materially realised biological relations; Scale identifies their relevant explanatory extent.

## Scale, Time, and the APS Triad

The relation between Scale, time, and persistence becomes clearest within the APS explanatory architecture. APS distinguishes three analytic projections:

- **Agency** concerns what living systems do.
- **Process** concerns how continuity is maintained despite change.
- **Scale** concerns where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.

These projections concern **one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation**. They are not three components whose interaction produces persistence, nor does Scale integrate Agency and Process across biological domains. Rather, the projections give different explanatory priority to different questions about the same materially realised living organisation. Agency foregrounds viability-oriented organisational activity, Process foregrounds continuity through change, and Scale foregrounds the spatial and temporal extent across which that persistence is organised.

Organised persistence is therefore not an emergent product of an Agencyâ€“Processâ€“Scale interaction. It is the continuity of the living organisation that these analytic projections allow biology to investigate from complementary explanatory perspectives.

## Implications for Biological Explanation

Bringing Scale and temporal continuity together has several consequences for biological explanation. Biological persistence cannot be understood simply as material endurance because the relevant organisation is continually enacted and re-established, and the spatial and temporal boundaries of an explanation cannot always be assumed in advance. Those boundaries must instead be established from the explanandum and from the materially realised dependencies relevant to it.

Extending an explanation across more domains likewise does not automatically increase explanatory adequacy. A local explanation may be sufficient, while a more extended explanation is warranted only where additional relations make an explanatory difference to the target. For the same reason, spatial structure and spatial extent must not be conflated. Material spatial organisation can contribute causally or constitutively to biological phenomena; Scale identifies the explanatory extent across which such organisation is relevant.

Finally, differences among spatial and temporal extents do not establish a hierarchy of biological causation. Where wider organisation affects local activity, explanation must identify the materially implemented constraints and relations through which local conditions are altered. A wider domain does not supersede local causation merely by being wider.

## Explanatory Architecture

### Central Question

**How does materially realised living organisation maintain continuity through time, and across what spatial and temporal extents must that organisation be identified to explain its persistence?**

### Architectural Role

This Synthesis article connects organised persistence with temporal continuity and the APS projection of Scale. It does not establish Scale as an additional biological mechanism or treat time and Scale as co-constitutive components of living organisation. Temporal analysis concerns the continuity and transformation through which organisation persists, while Scale concerns where that persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents. The biological organisation itself performs the causal, regulatory, and coordinative work.

### Dependency on the Core Scale Article

The meaning of Scale used here is governed by the Core Scale article:

**Scale is the analytic projection concerned with where persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.**

Accordingly, this Synthesis article does not use Scale to denote an ontological level, a causal domain, a coordinating mechanism, a spatial structure, or an independently acting dimension of life. Material organisation can extend across multiple spatial and temporal extents without Scale itself becoming a material component of that organisation.

### Spatial-Organisation Comparator

Hermida and Ladyman (2026) provide a contemporary account of the biological importance of materially realised spatial structure. Their analysis helps clarify why position, configuration, boundary, orientation, and physical interaction can matter directly to biological organisation, but APS Scale should not be substituted for those material relations. Where spatial organisation itself explains the target, describing its extent in APS Scale terms does not by itself constitute additional explanatory gain. Any stronger APS contribution requires target-matched comparison.

### Position Within APS

The article therefore synthesises three closely connected questions without collapsing them:

**What persists?**  
Viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation.

**How does it persist?**  
Through ongoing organisational activity that maintains and re-establishes continuity despite change.

**Where is that persistence organised?**  
Across the spatial and temporal extents established by the organisation relevant to the explanandum.

Agency, Process, and Scale make different aspects of this single explanatory architecture explicit.

## Conclusion

Life exists through organised continuity. Living systems persist not because their material components remain unchanged, but because their organisation is continually enacted, maintained, modified, and re-established through time. That organisation is materially realised through processes, structures, constraints, boundaries, interactions, and environmental relations whose relevant spatial and temporal extents differ with the biological explanandum.

Time makes the continuity and transformation of living organisation explicit, while Scale makes its relevant extent explicit. Neither performs the causal work of persistence; living organisation does. APS therefore does not explain persistence as the product of interacting scales or as the outcome of independently acting Agency, Process, and Scale components. It explains one viability-oriented, constraint-closed organisation through complementary analytic projections.

**Life persists through organised continuity; Process asks how that continuity is maintained despite change, and Scale asks where that persistence is organised across spatial and temporal extents.**

## Why the Question Matters

Debates concerning natural selection have long centred on a deceptively simple question: what does selection actually act on? Evolutionary theory has variously proposed genes, traits, organisms, groups, populations, developmental systems, and ecological relationships as the primary objects of selection. These debates have often been motivated by a legitimate concern to identify the causal entities responsible for evolutionary change.

APS approaches the problem from a different perspective. Rather than beginning with candidate units of selection, it begins with the broader continuity architecture within which selection operates. Evolution is understood as the historical transformation of viability-oriented organisation, and natural selection is understood as one process contributing to that transformation. The central question therefore becomes not which component selection acts upon, but what forms of organised continuity selection differentially stabilises through time.

This shift matters because selection is frequently assigned explanatory responsibilities that exceed its actual role. Selection is often treated as though it generates organisation, explains adaptation, produces biological order, or accounts for the existence of living systems themselves. Yet selection can perform none of these functions independently. Before selection can operate, there must already exist systems capable of sustaining organised persistence across time. Selection therefore presupposes the existence of continuity before it can contribute to its historical transformation.

APS consequently reframes the traditional question. Instead of asking whether selection acts on genes, organisms, or populations, APS asks how selection contributes to the differential continuity of organised persistence across generations. This broader perspective reveals that the central evolutionary phenomenon is not the success of isolated components but the historical continuity of lineages of organised persistence whose organisation contributes differently to viability under changing conditions.

Understanding what selection acts on therefore requires understanding the continuity architecture within which selection operates. Only then can selection be assigned its proper explanatory role within evolutionary theory.

## Selection as a Dependent Process

Natural selection remains one of the most important explanatory concepts in evolutionary biology. APS fully retains its importance while clarifying the conditions under which it operates.

Selection is not a primary generative process. It does not create organisation, generate viability, establish persistence, or explain the emergence of living systems. Rather, it operates only within systems already capable of sustaining organised persistence across generations. Selection therefore depends upon organisational conditions whose existence it cannot itself explain.

This dependency is often obscured because evolutionary explanations frequently begin with populations of already existing organisms. Once such populations are assumed, selection appears to function as the principal explanatory force driving evolutionary change. APS instead asks how such populations become possible in the first place. Before differences can be filtered, there must already exist viable systems capable of maintaining themselves, reproducing continuity, and generating variation across generations.

Selection therefore presupposes a broader continuity architecture. Biological agency sustains viability-oriented activity. Viability enables organised persistence. Inheritance reproduces continuity across generations. Variation introduces differences into that continuity. Adaptation reorganises persistence under changing conditions. Only within this already established framework can selection begin to contribute to evolutionary transformation.

Natural selection thus functions as a dependent evolutionary cause. Its effects emerge only because living systems have already achieved the organisational continuity required for differential persistence to occur. Selection cannot operate in the absence of viability, inheritance, adaptation, and organised persistence because these processes establish the conditions under which continuity becomes available for differential stabilisation.

This reframing places selection in its proper explanatory position. Selection remains indispensable because it helps explain why some forms of organisation become historically more continuous than others. Yet it remains dependent upon organisational processes whose existence precedes its operation. Understanding selection therefore requires understanding the persistence-sustaining organisation upon which selection depends.

Selection consequently functions as an evolutionary cause only within lineages capable of sustaining organised biological persistence across generations. Without such continuity there is nothing for selection to differentially stabilise, and no evolutionary transformation can occur.

## What Selection Differentially Stabilises

If natural selection depends upon organised persistence, then what exactly does it differentially stabilise?

Traditional answers have often focused upon particular entities. Genes, traits, organisms, groups, and populations have each been proposed as the primary objects of selection. APS does not deny the importance of any of these biological entities. Instead, it argues that none adequately captures the deeper continuity upon which evolutionary transformation depends.

Selection does not primarily stabilise genes considered in isolation. Nor does it stabilise traits independently of the developmental, physiological, behavioural, and ecological systems in which those traits participate. What persists through evolutionary time is not a disconnected component but a historically continuous lineage of organised persistence whose organisation contributes differently to continuity across generations.

From this perspective, selection operates upon differences in the continuity of lineages of viability-oriented organisation. These differences arise through variation, are reproduced through inheritance, are reorganised through adaptation, and become visible through differences in fitness. Selection then contributes to the differential historical stabilisation of those differences.

This interpretation helps explain why genes cannot be treated as privileged causal units. Genes contribute to organised persistence, but their effects depend entirely upon the broader systems within which they operate. Likewise, traits contribute to continuity only through their participation in organised biological activity. Selection therefore cannot be understood adequately by focusing upon isolated components. Its effects emerge from differences in the continuity-producing capacities of integrated forms of biological organisation.

The object of selection is therefore best understood as organised continuity rather than isolated entities. More precisely, selection contributes to the differential stabilisation of lineages of organised persistence whose viability, adaptability, and continuity differ under particular developmental and ecological conditions. What becomes historically continuous is not a component alone but a pattern of organisation capable of sustaining continuity across generations.

This reframing also clarifies why selection is inseparable from history. Selection does not simply evaluate biological organisation at a single moment in time. It contributes to the historical retention, amplification, or decline of lineages whose organisation generates different degrees of continuity. The phenomenon being stabilised is therefore fundamentally temporal. Selection acts within the ongoing continuity of living systems and contributes to how that continuity is transformed across evolutionary time.

## Selection, Fitness, and Lineage Continuity

The relationship between selection and fitness becomes clearer once both concepts are situated within the broader continuity architecture of APS.

Fitness concerns differences in the continuity of lineages of persistence-sustaining organisation. Some forms of organisation contribute more effectively to continuity across generations than others, producing differences in the historical persistence of lineages. Fitness therefore identifies differences in continuity among viable forms of organised persistence.

Natural selection does not create those differences. Rather, it contributes to their historical stabilisation. Selection operates because differences in continuity already exist, and its evolutionary significance derives from the fact that such differences influence which lineages remain historically represented through time.

This distinction is important because fitness and selection are often treated as interchangeable concepts. APS instead assigns them complementary explanatory roles. Fitness concerns differential continuity. Selection concerns the differential stabilisation of that continuity. Fitness identifies differences among lineages of organised persistence, whereas selection helps explain how those differences become historically amplified across generations.

The relationship becomes clearer when viewed within the broader continuity architecture of evolution. Inheritance reproduces continuity across generations and sustains lineages of organised persistence. Variation introduces differences into that continuity. Adaptation reorganises persistence under changing conditions. Fitness reflects differences in the continuity of viable lineages. Natural selection then differentially stabilises those differences through historical time. Evolutionary transformation emerges from the cumulative consequences of this process.

Selection therefore occupies neither the beginning nor the end of evolutionary explanation. It operates within an already existing framework of continuity-producing processes and contributes to the long-term transformation of that framework. Understanding selection requires understanding the lineages whose continuity it differentially stabilises, the fitness differences that make such stabilisation possible, and the organised persistence that makes both fitness and selection intelligible in the first place.

Seen in this way, natural selection is best understood not as a force acting upon isolated entities but as a process contributing to the differential historical continuity of lineages of organised persistence. It remains indispensable to evolutionary explanation, yet its significance becomes clearest when situated within the broader architecture of continuity through which life persists and transforms across time.

## Beyond Gene-Centric Selection

Gene-centric approaches have played an enormously important role in modern evolutionary biology. Population genetics has provided powerful tools for understanding evolutionary dynamics, and gene-focused models have often generated highly successful predictions concerning evolutionary change. APS does not reject these achievements. Instead, it seeks to clarify the explanatory assumptions that underlie them.

The central difficulty arises when genes are treated not merely as important participants in evolutionary processes but as the primary objects upon which selection acts. Such interpretations risk attributing explanatory primacy to one component of biological organisation while neglecting the broader systems that make genetic effects possible.

Genes do not operate independently. Their effects emerge through developmental organisation, physiological regulation, behavioural activity, ecological interaction, and organismâ€“environment coupling. The evolutionary consequences of genetic variation therefore depend upon the persistence-sustaining organisation within which genetic processes participate. Selection cannot act upon genes in abstraction because genes contribute to continuity only through the organised systems that sustain their biological significance.

APS consequently reframes gene-centric explanations within a broader organisational context. Genes remain indispensable contributors to continuity, inheritance, and evolutionary transformation, but they do not constitute privileged evolutionary units. Selection contributes to the differential stabilisation of lineages of organised persistence, and genetic processes participate in that larger continuity-producing architecture rather than replacing it.

This perspective preserves the empirical strengths of gene-centred research while avoiding reductionism. Genetic explanations remain important because genes contribute to continuity. They do not become foundational simply because they are measurable, heritable, or evolutionarily consequential. What ultimately persists through evolutionary history is not a gene alone but a lineage of organised persistence whose continuity depends upon the coordinated activity of many interacting processes.

[[box:gene-centric-vs-aps-grammar]]

## Selection and Multiscale Organisation

Selection is inherently multiscale because organised persistence is itself distributed across multiple interacting scales of biological organisation. Evolutionary outcomes emerge through relationships among physiological processes, developmental systems, organisms, ecological interactions, populations, and lineages extending through time. Selection therefore cannot be adequately understood by isolating any single scale of organisation as its exclusive object.

At developmental scales, organisational differences influence how continuity is generated and maintained throughout the life history of organisms. At physiological scales, viability depends upon regulatory processes that sustain persistence under changing conditions. At ecological scales, continuity depends upon interactions between organisms and the environments in which they persist. At lineage scales, continuity becomes visible through the historical persistence of forms of organisation across generations.

These scales do not operate independently. Development influences physiology, physiology affects ecological interaction, ecological conditions shape evolutionary possibilities, and evolutionary transformations alter future developmental trajectories. Selection therefore emerges from the consequences of interactions distributed across biological organisation rather than from isolated processes acting at a single scale.

This multiscale perspective helps clarify why debates concerning units of selection often prove difficult to resolve. Different investigators frequently focus upon different scales of continuity, each identifying important aspects of evolutionary organisation. APS does not deny the reality of these perspectives. Rather, it argues that their significance derives from their contribution to organised persistence within a larger continuity architecture.

Selection is therefore best understood as operating upon the outcomes of multiscale biological organisation. The continuity of lineages depends upon interactions distributed across developmental, physiological, behavioural, ecological, and evolutionary domains, and selection contributes to the differential stabilisation of those continuity-producing relationships through historical time.

## Selection Within the APS Evolutionary Architecture

APS situates natural selection within a broader explanatory framework organised around continuity, persistence, and transformation. Selection remains essential, but it is no longer treated as the primary source of biological order. Instead, it occupies a specific position within an already established architecture of continuity-producing processes.

Biological agency sustains viability-oriented activity. Viability enables organised persistence. Organised persistence establishes the continuity required for living systems to remain historically present. Inheritance reproduces continuity across generations and sustains lineages of organised persistence. Variation introduces differences into that continuity. Adaptation reorganises persistence under changing conditions. Fitness reflects differences in the continuity of viable lineages. Natural selection then differentially stabilises those differences through evolutionary time, contributing to the long-term transformation of biological organisation.

Within this architecture, selection performs a distinctive but limited role. It does not explain why living systems exist, how viability is maintained, how organisation emerges, or how continuity is reproduced. These processes are established through agency, viability, inheritance, development, and adaptation. Selection contributes by influencing which forms of organised continuity become historically stabilised under particular conditions.

This reframing resolves a number of longstanding difficulties in evolutionary explanation. It preserves the explanatory importance of selection while preventing it from being assigned responsibilities that belong elsewhere. Selection remains indispensable because evolutionary transformation depends upon differential continuity. Yet differential continuity itself presupposes organised persistence, viability, inheritance, and fitness. Selection therefore operates within an explanatory framework that is broader than selection itself.

[[box:structure-of-evolutionary-explanation]]

## From Selection to Evolutionary Explanation

The question of what selection acts upon has often been treated as a debate concerning genes, traits, organisms, groups, or populations. APS reframes the issue by shifting attention from isolated entities to organised continuity. The central evolutionary phenomenon is not the success of individual components but the differential historical continuity of lineages of organised persistence.

This shift has important explanatory consequences. It clarifies why selection cannot generate organisation, viability, or persistence. It explains why genes are evolutionarily significant without becoming privileged causal agents. It illuminates the relationship between fitness and selection, and it integrates developmental, physiological, ecological, and evolutionary processes within a common continuity architecture.

Selection therefore becomes intelligible as one component of a broader explanatory grammar. Living systems remain viable through organised persistence. Continuity is reproduced through inheritance, modified through variation, reorganised through adaptation, and differentiated through fitness. Selection then contributes to the differential historical stabilisation of those differences, shaping the trajectories through which lineages persist and transform across time.

Understanding selection in this way allows evolutionary explanation to move beyond disputes concerning isolated units and toward a richer account of how continuity is maintained and transformed across biological history.

Natural selection in APS is the differential stabilisation of lineages of viability-oriented organisation. # Semiosis â€” How Differences Come to Matter in Living Systems

## Introduction

Semiosis is traditionally concerned with signs and the relations through which something functions for a system in relation to something else. In philosophy, linguistics, semiotics, and cognitive science, such relations have often been associated with interpretation, communication, representation, and meaning. Biosemiotics extends the question into biology, asking whether and how sign processes participate in living organisation.

This extension presents an important explanatory problem. If semiosis is restricted to language, symbolic thought, or conscious interpretation, potentially important sign relations in non-human and non-cognitive biological systems may be excluded in advance. If semiosis is broadened until every biological response, signal, or causal correlation counts as semiotic, however, the concept risks losing explanatory discrimination.

APS approaches this problem by first distinguishing **biological significance from semiosis**.

Biological agency is viability-oriented organisational activity. Because conditions differ in how they bear upon continued functioning, living systems modulate activity differently in relation to them. **Biological Evaluation is the process through which agency generates significance.** A difference can therefore matter biologically without the additional claim that it functions as a sign.

Semiosis becomes a further explanatory question. APS uses the concept where a biologically significant difference appears to function within living organisation **in relation to another condition, object, possibility, or state of affairs**. The semiotic claim is therefore stronger than the claim that a system is causally sensitive to a difference or that the difference carries information.

This distinction also prevents semiosis from becoming an automatic bridge to meaning, representation, or cognition. APS does not posit a compulsory sequence in which evaluation produces semiosis, semiosis produces meaning, meaning produces information, information produces representation, and representation produces cognition. These concepts identify distinguishable explanatory relations whose connections must be established in particular cases.

The central question of this article is consequently:

> **When does a biologically significant difference function as a sign, and what explanatory work is gained by treating the relation as semiotic?**

[[box:aps-box-semiosis-is-operational]]

[[box:aps-box-meaning-develops-from-evaluative-significance]]

## Where This Article Fits

This Core article occupies a controlled position among the APS treatments of Biological Evaluation, significance, information, cognition, representation, and meaning.

**Biological Evaluation** owns the prior explanatory question of how differences come to matter biologically. Evaluation generates significance because conditions differ in how they bear upon viability. The existence of such significance does not by itself establish semiosis.

The present article asks the further question of when an already significant difference becomes organised in a specifically **sign-relational** form. Semiosis is therefore not the source of biological significance but a possible organisation of significant relations.

*Information in Biology â€” An APS Clarification* asks a different question again. Informational relations can exist through statistical or causal dependence without automatically becoming either biologically significant or semiotic. Some information-bearing differences may participate in sign relations; others need not.

*Cognition â€” Where Does It Belong in Biology?* concerns the organisation of biological significance across time. APS does not currently define cognition through semiosis, although semiotic relations may contribute to cognitive organisation in particular systems.

*Representation â€” When and Whether It Arises in Biological Systems* applies a stronger diagnostic test to states or organisations proposed to stand in for, model, or carry content concerning something beyond their immediate occurrence. Semiosis and representation may overlap, but neither concept is reducible to the other.

Finally, *Meaning in Biology â€” An APS Clarification* establishes that biological significance is not yet meaning. Meaning concerns the later interpretive organisation of what matters and should not be used as a synonym for semiosis.

The resulting architecture is deliberately non-linear:

**Significance â‰  Semiosis â‰  Meaning â‰  Representation.**

These distinctions do not imply complete independence. They prevent one concept from doing the explanatory work of another before their relationship has been established.

## Biological Significance Before Semiotic Commitment

The first control on an APS account of semiosis is that biological significance does not require semiosis.

Living systems encounter innumerable physical differences. Some make no relevant difference to their activity. Others alter conditions bearing upon viability and consequently modulate what the system does. Through Biological Evaluation, such differences acquire significance relative to the organisation of the living system.

A nutrient concentration may affect microbial activity. Temperature may alter physiological regulation. A developmental condition may modify a cellular trajectory. A chemical difference may influence immune activity. These differences can be biologically significant because of their effects on continued functioning.

Nothing in that description yet requires them to be signs.

This distinction matters because otherwise every viability-relevant causal relation becomes semiotic by definition. The term *semiosis* would then add little to Biological Evaluation. It would simply rename the fact that differences matter to living systems.

APS therefore separates two questions:

**Does the difference matter to the living system?**

and:

**Does the difference function for that system in relation to something beyond itself?**

The first concerns biological significance. The second introduces the semiotic question.

This makes semiosis a substantive explanatory hypothesis rather than an automatic property of life.

[[box:aps-box-viability-grounds-evaluation]]

## What Makes a Relation Semiotic?

A sign is not merely a difference that causes another difference.

Physical systems are filled with causal relations. Temperature alters pressure; light triggers chemical reactions; one molecular state changes another. Such relations can carry information in a statistical or causal sense without necessarily being semiotic.

The semiotic question arises when a state or difference functions within an organised system **in relation to something other than itself**.

Consider a biological signal. Its immediate physical effect may be fully describable through molecular interaction. Yet the same state may also function within the organism because its occurrence indicates another condition, initiates activity appropriate to that condition, or participates in an organised relation whose biological role depends upon what the signal signifies rather than solely upon its local physical properties.

The distinction is subtle but important. A semiotic explanation proposes more than causal efficacy. It proposes a relation among a sign-bearing state, what that state functions in relation to, and the organisation through which that relation affects activity.

APS does not require this relation to be symbolic, linguistic, conscious, or representational in the stronger cognitive sense. A sign relation may be materially implemented in physiological, developmental, behavioural, or other biological organisation.

Neither should the semiotic relation be inferred merely from scientific description. Scientists routinely use one measurable state as an indicator of another. The fact that *we* treat a molecular concentration as a sign of disease, for example, does not establish that the concentration functions semiotically within the organism itself.

The explanatory task is therefore to identify the sign relation **within the organisation of the biological system**.

## A Diagnostic Test for Semiotic Explanation

APS does not presently propose universal necessary and sufficient conditions for semiosis. Different semiotic theories disagree about the structure and scope of sign relations, and biological cases may realise them in different ways.

APS can nevertheless identify diagnostic considerations that make a semiotic interpretation stronger or weaker.

A semiotic explanation becomes more strongly warranted where:

1. **A materially identifiable sign-vehicle or sign-bearing state can be specified.**  
   The proposed sign must be realised within the biological system rather than existing only in the description supplied by an observer.

2. **The sign functions in relation to something beyond itself.**  
   Its biological role depends upon another condition, object, relation, possibility, or state of affairs rather than being exhausted by its immediate physical effects.

3. **The system's activity depends upon that sign relation.**  
   The proposed sign must make a difference to biological organisation because of the relation in which it participates, not merely because it is causally active.

4. **The relation is not exhausted by simple causal covariance or information-bearing correlation.**  
   Treating the state as a sign should explain something that would otherwise remain unexplained by a weaker causal or informational description.

5. **Context can alter the significance or use of the sign relation.**  
   A state may function differently according to the organisation, history, developmental condition, or current circumstances of the system, supporting the claim that its role is relational rather than fixed solely by physical form.

6. **Successful and failed sign-use can in principle be distinguished.**  
   Where a proposed sign relation can be used appropriately or inappropriately, or can fail to guide activity in relation to what it signifies, the semiotic interpretation gains additional explanatory content.

7. **Semiotic description provides explanatory gain.**  
   The attribution should identify a dependency relevant to the specified explanandum that is not already adequately captured by biological significance, causal regulation, signal transmission, or information alone.

These considerations are diagnostic rather than a scoring system. No single item automatically establishes semiosis, and APS does not presently claim that every genuine sign relation must realise each consideration in precisely the same form.

Their purpose is methodological: to prevent semiotic terminology from replacing explanation.

A semiotic claim should therefore identify **what functions as the sign, what it functions in relation to, how that relation is materially implemented, what difference it makes, and why describing the relation as semiotic improves the explanation**.

## Semiosis and Biological Significance

Semiosis depends upon biological significance in a limited explanatory sense: a proposed biological sign relation must matter to the organisation of the living system if it is to count as biological semiosis.

This does not mean that significance is generated by semiosis.

A difference becomes significant through Biological Evaluation because it bears upon viability-oriented activity. A semiotic relation becomes possible when such a difference acquires a further relational roleâ€”for example, when its occurrence functions in relation to another condition and modulates activity accordingly.

This provides a way of understanding why the same physical difference can matter differently in different biological contexts. A chemical state may function as a sign in one organism or developmental condition while having no comparable role in another. Even within the same organism, the significance and use of a signal can change with physiological condition, developmental history, environmental context, or prior activity.

Significance is therefore relationally real without being intrinsic to the physical difference considered in isolation.

Semiosis adds a further relation: the significant difference functions **as a sign of, for, or in relation to something else** within the organisation of the system.

This is why APS should not say that semiosis transforms meaningless physical differences into biological significance. Biological Evaluation already explains the emergence of significance. Semiosis asks what happens when significant differences acquire sign-relational organisation.

## Semiosis Is Not Meaning

The distinction between semiosis and meaning is especially important because the two concepts are frequently associated within semiotic and biosemiotic traditions.

APS does not deny that sign relations can participate in meaning. It rejects the stronger inference that every biological sign relation is already meaningful in the richer sense developed within the APS cognitionâ€“mind architecture.

Biological significance identifies what matters to a living system because conditions differ in how they bear upon viability. Semiosis concerns sign-relational organisation of such differences. Meaning concerns the interpretive organisation of what matters.

These explanatory relations may become increasingly integrated within cognitive systems, minds, language, culture, and reflective agency. Their possible integration does not justify identifying them at their biological origin.

A signal can therefore participate in a semiotic relation without APS having to say that the organism possesses meaning in the same sense in which meaning is attributed to interpretive cognitive organisation. Conversely, meaningful activity may involve many semiotic and representational relations without meaning being reducible to the presence of signs.

The distinction also protects biosemiotic language from anthropomorphic overextension. Terms such as *interpretation* and *meaning-making* have legitimate theoretical histories, but when applied to minimal biological systems they can suggest cognitive or experiential capacities that the evidence does not establish.

APS therefore uses them cautiously.

Where biosemiotic theories describe living systems as meaning-making systems, APS can recognise the theoretical importance of that claim while distinguishing it from its own narrower account. Within APS, **biological significance is not yet meaning, and semiosis is not by definition meaning-making**.

[[box:aps-box-meaning-develops-from-evaluative-significance]]

## Semiosis and Information

Information and semiosis should likewise remain distinct.

A relation can carry information without functioning as a sign for the biological system. Statistical dependence, causal covariance, sequence structure, and signal transmission can all support legitimate informational descriptions without requiring semiotic interpretation.

Conversely, some information-bearing relations may participate in semiosis. A signal may reliably covary with another condition and, within the organisation of the living system, function in relation to that condition. In such cases informational and semiotic descriptions can concern different aspects of the same materially realised relation.

The important point is that neither concept should be made universally prior to the other.

APS therefore does not claim that information generates semiosis, nor that semiosis universally grounds information. Instead it asks what kind of relation is being described.

If the explanandum concerns statistical dependence, coding structure, transmission, or uncertainty reduction, an informational explanation may be appropriate without semiotic commitment. If the explanandum concerns how one significant state functions for the system in relation to another condition, a semiotic explanation may add something further.

This distinction also prevents the familiar language of *signals*, *codes*, and *messages* from settling the issue prematurely. These terms can be scientifically useful without implying that every information-bearing process constitutes semiosis.

The relation between information and semiosis must therefore be established in the case being investigated rather than derived from a universal conceptual sequence.

## Semiosis and Representation

Semiosis and representation can overlap, but they should not be equated.

A semiotic relation requires some state or difference to function in relation to something beyond itself. A representational claim is typically stronger: it proposes that some materially realised state or organisation stands in for, models, or carries content concerning something in a way that contributes distinctively to cognition or behaviour.

Some sign relations may therefore be representational. Others may operate through more immediate biological signalling or relational organisation without satisfying the stronger diagnostics for representation.

The reverse inference should also be avoided. APS does not currently require all possible representation to be derived from a prior semiotic stage.

The dedicated article *Representation â€” When and Whether It Arises in Biological Systems* asks when content-bearing or stand-in relations add explanatory work beyond biological significance, information, memory, anticipation, or cognition alone. The present article asks the narrower question of when a significant difference functions sign-relationally.

The distinction can be summarised as follows:

**Significance asks what matters.**

**Semiosis asks whether something significant functions as a sign in relation to something else.**

**Representation asks whether some state or organisation functions as a content-bearing stand-in or model in a way that adds explanatory work.**

These formulations distinguish the questions without predetermining how their answers will relate in every biological system.

## Semiosis and Cognition

APS does not define cognition through semiosis.

Cognition is **the organisation of biological significance across time**. More diagnostically:

> Biological agency becomes cognitive when integrated biological significance modulates activity across a temporal field of viability-relevant possibilities in ways not exhausted by immediate or fixed regulation.

Semiotic relations may participate in this organisation. A cognitive system may use signs concerning remembered conditions, anticipated possibilities, social relations, environmental opportunities, or other states that are not reducible to immediate causal stimulation.

It does not follow that cognition must always be semiotic.

A system might organise biological significance across time through learned dispositions, dynamically integrated sensorimotor relations, or other forms of cognitive organisation without the available evidence warranting a distinct sign-relational description.

Nor does semiosis automatically establish cognition. A biological sign relation may contribute to regulation without exhibiting the temporal integration, counterfactual depth, or flexibility required by the APS cognition boundary.

The relationship must therefore be investigated rather than stipulated.

Where semiotic organisation contributes to cognition, the relevant question is what the sign relation adds to the system's organisation of significance across time. Where cognition can be explained adequately without semiotic commitment, APS should not introduce semiosis merely to complete a conceptual sequence.

  <a href="/assets/diagrams/cognition-visual.png" target="_blank" rel="noopener">

  </p>
